question: A team trains a computer vision model on 40 TB of images stored in Amazon S3. Each epoch must read the full dataset, and GPU utilization drops because the training instances wait for data. The team wants a high-throughput shared file system that stays in sync with the S3 bucket. Which storage option will meet these requirements?
options: Amazon EFS with the Bursting throughput mode
Amazon S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval for the training images
Amazon EBS Provisioned IOPS volumes attached to each training instance
Amazon FSx for Lustre linked to the S3 bucket
explanations: EFS is a general-purpose shared file system; bursting throughput is sized for spiky workloads, not sustained parallel reads of tens of terabytes.
Glacier Instant Retrieval lowers storage cost for rarely accessed data; it doesn’t increase read throughput for training.
EBS volumes attach to individual instances, so each node would need its own copy of the 40 TB dataset.
FSx for Lustre is built for high-throughput, low-latency parallel access and can lazy-load and sync data from a linked S3 bucket.
takeaway: Sustained, parallel, high-throughput reads of S3 training data → FSx for Lustre linked to S3.

question: A SageMaker AI training job uses a 2 TB dataset in Amazon S3. Logs show that the job spends 35 minutes downloading data before the first training step starts. The training script reads files sequentially. Which change will reduce the startup time with the LEAST effort?
options: Copy the dataset to a larger Amazon EBS volume before each training job
Switch the instance type to one with more GPUs
Compress the dataset into a single archive file in S3
Configure the training input channel to use FastFile mode so data streams from S3
explanations: Copying the data adds another full transfer step instead of removing one.
More GPUs don’t speed up the download that happens before training starts.
A single large archive still has to be downloaded (and extracted) before the script can read it.
FastFile mode streams objects from S3 on demand through a file system interface, so training starts without downloading the whole dataset.
takeaway: File mode downloads everything first; FastFile (or Pipe) mode streams from S3 so training starts sooner.

question: A data engineering team stores 3 years of transaction data in Amazon S3 as CSV files. ML engineers query a handful of columns with Amazon Athena to build training datasets, and query costs keep rising. Which change will MOST reduce the amount of data scanned?
options: Convert the files to Apache Parquet with Snappy compression
Compress the CSV files with gzip
Split the CSV files into many smaller objects
Convert the files to JSON Lines with one record per line
explanations: Parquet is columnar, so Athena reads only the columns a query needs, and compression shrinks them further.
Compression reduces bytes scanned somewhat, but every column is still read.
Small files add overhead and don’t reduce the columns scanned.
JSON is row-oriented and usually larger than CSV, so Athena still scans whole records.
takeaway: Query a few columns of large data → columnar formats (Parquet or ORC).

question: A retailer sends clickstream events as JSON to AWS. The ML team needs the events delivered to Amazon S3 in Apache Parquet format every few minutes for model training. The team doesn’t want to manage servers or write conversion code. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Use Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink to write each event to S3 as JSON
Use Amazon SQS with an AWS Lambda function that converts each message to Parquet
Use Amazon Data Firehose with record format conversion to Parquet
Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with an Amazon EC2 consumer that writes Parquet files
explanations: Flink is for stateful stream processing, and this design still writes JSON instead of Parquet.
Writing one Parquet file per message produces many tiny files and requires custom code.
Firehose buffers records, converts JSON to Parquet by using a Glue table schema, and delivers to S3 without servers.
This works but requires managing EC2 consumers and conversion code.
takeaway: Streaming JSON → Parquet in S3 with no code → Data Firehose record format conversion.

question: A ride-sharing company wants to compute, for each driver, the number of trips completed in the last 15 minutes from a stream of trip events. The aggregated values must be updated continuously and written to the SageMaker AI Feature Store online store. Which service should the company use to compute the aggregations?
options: Amazon Athena queries on a schedule
AWS Glue DataBrew recipe jobs
Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink
Amazon Data Firehose with data transformation enabled
explanations: Scheduled batch queries can’t keep features continuously up to date.
DataBrew runs batch recipe jobs on datasets, not continuous stream processing.
Flink provides stateful, windowed aggregations over streams, which suits rolling per-driver counts.
Firehose transformation is per-record and stateless; it can’t keep windowed counts per driver.
takeaway: Windowed, stateful streaming aggregations → Managed Service for Apache Flink.

question: A Kinesis data stream in provisioned mode ingests IoT sensor readings for an anomaly detection model. Producers receive ProvisionedThroughputExceededException errors, but CloudWatch shows that most shards are far below their limits while one shard is saturated. The partition key is the device model, and one model sends 70% of the traffic. Which change will resolve the errors?
options: Increase the stream’s data retention period
Switch producers to the PutRecord API instead of PutRecords
Add enhanced fan-out consumers to the stream
Use a high-cardinality partition key, such as each device’s ID
explanations: Retention controls how long records are kept, not write throughput.
Single-record writes increase API overhead and don’t fix a hot shard.
Enhanced fan-out improves read throughput for consumers, not write capacity per shard.
Spreading records across many partition keys distributes writes evenly across shards and removes the hot shard.
takeaway: A hot shard comes from a skewed partition key; use a high-cardinality key (or on-demand mode with a good key).

question: An ML engineer needs to join customer records in an Amazon RDS for MySQL database with purchase history stored as Parquet files in Amazon S3. The joined dataset must be refreshed every night and written to S3 for training. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: A scheduled AWS Glue ETL job with a JDBC connection
Export the RDS tables manually each night and join them with pandas in a SageMaker Studio notebook
Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to replicate RDS changes into S3
Run an Apache Spark cluster on Amazon EC2 that reads both sources
explanations: Glue is serverless Spark: it can read RDS through a connection and S3 data, join them, and run on a schedule.
Manual exports and notebooks are hard to schedule and maintain.
Kinesis is for streaming data; it doesn’t join a database with S3 files.
Self-managed Spark clusters add significant operational work.
takeaway: Scheduled joins across databases and S3 with no servers → AWS Glue ETL job.

topic: Vector store next to relational data
question: A company stores product data in Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. It wants to add semantic search over product descriptions by storing embeddings next to the existing product rows and joining them in SQL. The team prefers to avoid adding a new database service. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Store the embeddings in Amazon DynamoDB and join them with the product rows in the application
Create an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain for the embeddings and sync product IDs to it nightly
Store the embeddings in Amazon ElastiCache and refresh them hourly
Enable the pgvector extension in Aurora PostgreSQL and store the embeddings in a vector column
explanations: This adds a second database and moves the join into application code.
OpenSearch is a strong vector store but is a new service to run.
A cache adds another service and isn’t the system of record for joins.
pgvector adds vector types and similarity search to PostgreSQL, so embeddings live beside the relational data.
takeaway: Vectors alongside existing PostgreSQL data → pgvector on Aurora or RDS for PostgreSQL.

question: A legal firm generates embeddings for 400 million archived document chunks. Queries are infrequent, and sub-second latency is acceptable. The firm wants the lowest storage cost for the vectors and doesn’t want to manage clusters. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Amazon ElastiCache with vector search enabled
Amazon OpenSearch Service with UltraWarm nodes
Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector on large instances
Amazon S3 Vectors, with a vector index in a new vector bucket
explanations: In-memory storage is the most expensive way to keep hundreds of millions of rarely used vectors.
OpenSearch domains require cluster management and cost more for rarely queried vectors.
Provisioned database instances run continuously and are costly for rarely used data.
S3 Vectors is purpose-built, serverless vector storage with sub-second queries at a much lower cost for large, infrequently queried datasets.
takeaway: Huge, infrequently queried vector sets at the lowest cost → S3 Vectors.

question: A support portal needs search that combines exact keyword matches on error codes with semantic similarity on problem descriptions. The team expects to scale to millions of documents and wants to tune ranking of the combined results. Which TWO capabilities should the team use? (Select TWO.)
options: A Bedrock knowledge base set to the SEMANTIC search type, with no keyword component
OpenSearch k-NN vector fields for semantic similarity
OpenSearch lexical (BM25) queries combined with vector queries in a hybrid search
Amazon Athena queries with LIKE filters on the documents in S3
Amazon Redshift materialized views of the document text
explanations: Semantic-only retrieval can miss exact error codes; the requirement needs keyword and vector matching combined.
The k-NN plugin stores embeddings and runs approximate nearest neighbor search.
Hybrid search merges keyword relevance with vector similarity, which suits exact error codes plus meaning.
Athena is for SQL analytics, not low-latency ranked search.
Redshift is a data warehouse, not a search engine.
takeaway: Keyword + semantic ranking → OpenSearch hybrid search (BM25 + k-NN).

question: A media company is building a dataset for a multimodal model that uses podcast audio files, cover images, and episode transcripts. Each episode also has metadata such as genre and duration that the training pipeline filters on. Which storage design is MOST appropriate?
options: Store the audio, images, and transcripts as BLOB columns in Amazon RDS
Store all files on an Amazon EBS volume that is attached to one training instance, with a metadata CSV
Store each episode’s files as attributes of a single Amazon DynamoDB item
S3 for the files plus a metadata table with S3 keys
explanations: Large binary objects in a relational database are costly and slow to stream for training.
A single EBS volume doesn’t scale or share well across pipelines.
DynamoDB items are limited to 400 KB, far too small for audio files.
S3 scales for large unstructured files, and a metadata table makes filtering and dataset assembly easy.
takeaway: Unstructured media in S3, plus a metadata index that points to the objects.

question: A manufacturer wants to stream live video from factory cameras to AWS so that a computer vision model can detect safety violations in near real time. Which AWS service should ingest the video streams?
options: Amazon Data Firehose
AWS DataSync
Amazon Kinesis Video Streams for the camera feeds
Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink
explanations: Firehose delivers records to destinations; it isn’t designed for live video ingestion and playback.
DataSync transfers files in bulk; it doesn’t ingest live streams.
Kinesis Video Streams securely ingests, stores, and serves live video for analytics and ML processing.
Flink processes record streams; it doesn’t ingest, store, and play back live video.
takeaway: Live camera video for ML → Kinesis Video Streams.

question: A fraud detection model reads features from the SageMaker AI Feature Store online store. A new feature, the number of card transactions in the last 5 minutes, is computed by an AWS Lambda function from a Kinesis data stream. How should the Lambda function write the feature so that it’s available for real-time inference within seconds?
options: Call the PutRecord API for the feature group
Write the values to Amazon S3 and run a nightly Feature Store batch ingestion job
Send the values to an Amazon SNS topic that the endpoint subscribes to
Write the values to the offline store’s S3 location directly
explanations: PutRecord writes to the online store immediately (and to the offline store if it is enabled), so the value is available for low-latency reads.
Nightly batch ingestion is far too slow for a 5-minute feature.
Endpoints don’t subscribe to SNS topics for features.
Writing files into the offline store doesn’t update the online store.
takeaway: Streaming feature updates → PutRecord into the online store.

question: Data scientists need a point-in-time correct training dataset built from several feature groups in SageMaker AI Feature Store. They want to use SQL without exporting data manually. Which approach should they use?
options: Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights on the Feature Store logs
Read the feature groups with Amazon DynamoDB Scan operations
Query the offline store tables with Athena
Query the online store with the GetRecord API for each record ID and timestamp in the dataset
explanations: Logs don’t contain the feature values in a queryable training format.
Feature Store isn’t accessed through DynamoDB APIs.
The offline store keeps historical records in S3 with Glue Data Catalog tables, so Athena can join feature groups by event time.
The online store holds latest values only and is meant for low-latency single lookups.
takeaway: Historical, point-in-time training data → offline store queried with Athena.

question: A healthcare company stores training data in Amazon S3. Compliance rules require that the data is encrypted at rest with keys that the company controls, and that the company can audit every use of the keys. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: SSE-KMS with a customer managed key
Use client-side encryption with a static key that is stored in the training script
Store the data in S3 Glacier Deep Archive
Enable server-side encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys (SSE-S3)
explanations: A customer managed KMS key gives the company control of the key policy and logs every use in AWS CloudTrail.
Embedding keys in code is insecure and can’t be audited.
Changing the storage class doesn’t change who controls the encryption keys.
SSE-S3 keys are managed by AWS; the company can’t control or audit individual key use.
takeaway: Customer-controlled, auditable keys → SSE-KMS with a customer managed key.

question: An ML engineer needs a full copy of a 2 TB Amazon DynamoDB table in Amazon S3 for model training. The table serves production traffic, and the export must not consume the table’s read capacity. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Enable DynamoDB Streams and use an AWS Lambda function to copy each item to Amazon S3
Increase read capacity and run parallel Query operations
DynamoDB export to S3 (with PITR enabled)
Run a Scan operation from an AWS Glue job and write the results to S3
explanations: Streams capture changes from now on; they don’t produce a full copy of existing items.
This still consumes capacity and adds cost.
Table export reads from point-in-time recovery backups, so it doesn’t use read capacity.
A Scan reads through the table’s capacity and can throttle production traffic.
takeaway: Full DynamoDB copy to S3 without using read capacity → export to S3 (needs PITR).

question: A company has 80 TB of labeled images on an on-premises NFS server and wants to move them to Amazon S3 once for model training. The transfer should be automated, encrypted in transit, and verify data integrity. Which service should the company use?
options: AWS Storage Gateway Tape Gateway
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
AWS DataSync
Amazon Data Firehose
explanations: Tape Gateway is for backup software that writes to virtual tapes.
Kinesis ingests streaming records, not existing file shares.
DataSync automates online transfers from NFS or SMB to S3, encrypts data in transit, and verifies integrity.
Firehose delivers streaming records, not bulk file transfers.
takeaway: Bulk online transfer from NFS/SMB to S3 → DataSync.

question: Training data in Amazon S3 is queried with Amazon Athena, and most queries filter on event date. Queries scan the entire dataset each time. Which change will MOST reduce query cost and time?
options: Increase the query concurrency limit of the Athena workgroup that runs the queries
Partition by date and register the partitions
Move the data to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access
Store all objects under a single prefix
explanations: Concurrency doesn’t change how much data each query scans.
Partition pruning lets Athena skip objects for dates the query doesn’t need.
Storage class affects storage cost, not data scanned.
A flat layout forces Athena to read every object.
takeaway: Filter on a column often → partition by it so Athena prunes data.

question: An AWS Glue Spark job that prepares training data has started failing with out-of-memory errors on executors after the input data grew from 50 GB to 900 GB. The job reprocesses all historical files every night, although only new files arrive each day. Which TWO actions will resolve the failures and reduce cost? (Select TWO.)
options: Increase spark.driver.memory while keeping the same worker type and count
Store the input data in S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
Use a larger worker type, such as G.2X, or add workers
Repartition the output into fewer, larger files at the end of the job
Enable job bookmarks so that each run processes only new files
explanations: The errors are on executors, so more driver memory doesn’t help, and the job still reprocesses all history.
Archived data must be restored before Glue can read it.
Larger workers give each executor more memory, and more workers spread the data.
Output file sizes don’t change executor memory pressure on the 900 GB input.
Bookmarks track processed data, so nightly runs read just the new files.
takeaway: Glue OOM → bigger/more workers; reprocessing everything → job bookmarks for incremental runs.

question: A data pipeline writes millions of 5 KB JSON files to Amazon S3 each day. Downstream SageMaker AI processing jobs that read the data are slow, and most of the job time is spent listing and opening objects. Which change will MOST improve read performance?
options: Compact them into larger Parquet files
Enable S3 Versioning on the bucket
Move the objects to S3 Standard-Infrequent Access
Turn on S3 Transfer Acceleration for the bucket that the processing jobs read from
explanations: Fewer, larger columnar files cut per-object request overhead and speed up reads.
Versioning keeps object history and adds objects instead of reducing them.
Storage class doesn’t change per-request overhead.
Transfer Acceleration speeds long-distance uploads, not in-Region reads of many small objects.
takeaway: Lots of tiny objects → compact into larger (columnar) files.

question: Business analysts need to clean a sales dataset in Amazon S3 by removing duplicates, fixing date formats, and filling missing values. They don’t write code and want to save the steps as a reusable recipe. Which service should they use?
options: AWS Glue DataBrew with saved recipes
Amazon EMR with Apache Spark
AWS Lambda
Amazon Athena
explanations: DataBrew is a visual data preparation tool with 250+ transforms that are saved as reusable recipes.
EMR requires writing Spark code and managing clusters.
Lambda requires code.
Athena runs SQL queries; it isn’t a visual cleaning tool with recipes.
takeaway: Visual, no-code cleaning with reusable recipes → Glue DataBrew.

question: An ML engineer built a sequence of transformations in SageMaker Data Wrangler (in SageMaker Canvas) and wants the same transformations to run automatically each week on new data as part of a training workflow. Which approach requires the LEAST rework?
options: Take screenshots of the flow and reimplement it in a Lambda function
Export the Data Wrangler flow to SageMaker Pipelines and schedule the pipeline
Run the transformations manually in Canvas each week
Rewrite the transformations as an AWS Glue DataBrew recipe
explanations: Manual reimplementation is error-prone and slow.
Data Wrangler flows can be exported to processing jobs or pipelines, so the same steps run on a schedule.
Manual runs don’t automate the workflow.
Rebuilding the flow in another tool is unnecessary rework.
takeaway: Reuse Data Wrangler transforms in production → export the flow to Pipelines or a processing job.

question: A company has hundreds of existing PySpark feature engineering scripts that use custom Spark configurations and third-party JAR libraries. It needs to run them on petabytes of data in Amazon S3 with full control over the cluster configuration. Which service is the BEST fit?
options: Amazon EMR
Amazon Athena
Amazon Data Firehose
AWS Glue DataBrew
explanations: EMR runs Apache Spark with full control of cluster configuration, custom JARs, and large-scale processing.
Athena runs SQL queries, not arbitrary PySpark scripts with custom JARs.
Firehose delivers streaming data and can’t run batch Spark jobs.
DataBrew uses visual recipes and can’t run existing PySpark scripts.
takeaway: Existing Spark code + full cluster control at scale → Amazon EMR.

question: A feature that records customer annual spend is heavily right-skewed: most values are small, but a few are very large. A linear model trained on it performs poorly. Which transformation is MOST appropriate for this feature?
options: Min-max scaling to the range 0 to 1
Label encoding
A log transformation of the spend values
One-hot encoding
explanations: Min-max scaling changes the range but keeps the skewed shape of the distribution.
Label encoding maps categories to integers and doesn’t address skew.
A log transform compresses large values and makes right-skewed distributions more symmetric.
One-hot encoding is for categorical features, not continuous amounts.
takeaway: Right-skewed positive values → log transform.

question: An ML engineer trains a k-nearest neighbors model on features that include age (18–90) and annual income (20,000–2,000,000). The model ignores age almost entirely. What should the engineer do before training?
options: Apply one-hot encoding to both features
Standardize or normalize the features so they have comparable scales
Remove the age feature because it has a small range
Increase the value of k
explanations: These are continuous values, not categories.
Distance-based algorithms are dominated by large-scale features unless features are scaled.
The issue is scale, not usefulness; scaling keeps the feature’s information.
Changing k doesn’t fix the imbalance between feature scales.
takeaway: KNN, k-means, and other distance-based methods need scaled features.

question: A marketing model uses customer age as a feature. The business team believes that purchase behavior changes in stages, such as 18–25, 26–40, and 41–65, rather than year by year. Which feature engineering technique matches this belief?
options: Binning
Standardization
Log transformation
Feature hashing
explanations: Binning turns a continuous value into ordered groups that match the stages.
Standardization rescales values but keeps them continuous.
A log transform changes the shape of the distribution, not the grouping.
Hashing maps high-cardinality categories into a fixed number of buckets.
takeaway: Continuous value with stage-like effects → binning.

question: A dataset includes a payment_method column with five values: card, cash, wallet, transfer, and voucher. The values have no natural order. The model is a linear learner. How should the column be encoded?
options: Min-max normalization
Binning
Ordinal (label) encoding as 1 to 5
One-hot encoding
explanations: Normalization applies to numeric values, not categories.
Binning groups continuous values into ranges.
Integer codes imply an order and distance that don’t exist for these values.
One-hot encoding creates a binary column per category without implying an order.
takeaway: Low-cardinality nominal categories → one-hot encoding.

question: A demand forecasting model receives an order_timestamp feature such as 2026-03-14T18:42:00Z. Demand depends strongly on the time of day and the day of the week. Which feature engineering step should the ML engineer take?
options: Convert the timestamp into a single integer that counts seconds since 1 January 1970
One-hot encode the full timestamp string
Drop the timestamp because models can’t use dates
Split it into hour of day and day of week
explanations: A raw epoch number hides daily and weekly cycles.
Nearly every timestamp is unique, so this creates useless high-cardinality columns.
The timestamp carries useful signal once it’s decomposed.
Feature splitting exposes the cyclical patterns the model needs.
takeaway: Timestamps → split into hour, day of week, month, and similar features.

question: Sensor readings arrive in an Amazon Kinesis data stream. Before the readings are stored, each record must be validated, converted from Fahrenheit to Celsius, and enriched with a site ID from a small lookup table. The logic is stateless. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: An Amazon EMR cluster running Spark Streaming
An AWS Glue crawler on the stream
A Lambda function triggered by the stream
A SageMaker AI processing job that runs every hour on the newest records
explanations: A long-running cluster is heavy for simple stateless transforms.
Crawlers infer schemas; they don’t transform records.
Lambda reads batches from the stream and applies simple per-record logic without servers.
Hourly batch jobs don’t process the stream continuously.
takeaway: Simple, stateless per-record stream transforms → Lambda with a Kinesis event source.

question: A company uses Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 to embed 50 million document chunks for a RAG application. Vector storage costs are too high. Retrieval quality tests show only a small drop in recall when the embeddings are smaller. Which change will MOST reduce storage cost?
options: Switch to a larger embedding model with more dimensions
Output 256 or 512 dimensions instead
Increase the chunk overlap so that each chunk carries more neighboring context
Store each embedding twice, once normalized and once raw
explanations: More dimensions increase storage cost.
Titan Text Embeddings V2 supports smaller output dimensions, which cut storage with a modest accuracy trade-off.
More overlap creates more or larger chunks, so storage grows.
Duplicating vectors doubles storage.
takeaway: Smaller embedding dimensions → lower vector storage and faster search, with a small accuracy trade-off.

question: An online store wants shoppers to search its catalog by uploading a photo or typing a description, and to retrieve matching products in both cases. Which approach should the ML engineer use to create the vectors?
options: Use two separate text embedding models with different dimensions
Use a text embedding model for descriptions and store the images as base64 strings next to them
Use Amazon Rekognition labels as the searchable field for each product
A multimodal model with one shared vector space
explanations: Vectors from different models and spaces can’t be compared.
Base64 text isn’t a meaningful embedding of the image content.
Labels lose detail and don’t support similarity search over descriptions.
A shared embedding space lets an image query match text and image vectors, and the reverse.
takeaway: Search across images and text → multimodal embeddings in one shared space.

question: An ML engineer fine-tunes an open-source language model on SageMaker AI. Validation loss is unexpectedly high, and the engineer finds that the dataset was pre-tokenized with a different model’s tokenizer. What should the engineer do?
options: Lowercase all text and keep the existing token IDs from the other tokenizer
Remove punctuation so that fewer tokens are produced
Re-tokenize with the base model’s tokenizer
Increase the number of training epochs
explanations: The token IDs are still from the wrong vocabulary.
This doesn’t align the tokens with the model.
Each model expects token IDs from its own vocabulary and tokenizer.
More epochs can’t fix tokens that don’t match the model’s vocabulary.
takeaway: Always tokenize with the base model’s own tokenizer.

question: A team is training an intent classifier for a telecom chatbot, but it has only 300 labeled examples for some intents. Collecting more labeled data will take months. Which TWO techniques can increase the variety of training examples for these intents? (Select TWO.)
options: Generating paraphrases with a foundation model and reviewing a sample of them
Applying TF-IDF weighting to the existing examples so that rare words get more importance
Back-translation, such as translating to another language and back with Amazon Translate
Oversampling the rare intents by repeating their existing examples until the classes are balanced
Converting the text to lowercase
explanations: LLM-generated paraphrases add variety; spot checks keep quality and labels correct.
TF-IDF changes how features are weighted; it doesn’t create new examples.
Back-translation produces paraphrases that keep the original label.
Repeated copies balance counts but add no new variety, and they encourage overfitting.
Normalization doesn’t add variety.
takeaway: Small text datasets → augmentation with back-translation or reviewed synthetic paraphrases.

question: A company is building a Bedrock knowledge base over long technical manuals with chapters, sections, and short procedures. Small chunks retrieve precise matches, but answers often lack the surrounding context of the section. Which chunking strategy will BEST address this?
options: Fixed-size chunking with zero overlap
No chunking, so each manual is a single chunk
Hierarchical chunking with parent and child chunks
Fixed-size chunking with a smaller chunk size
explanations: Removing overlap tends to split related sentences apart.
Whole manuals exceed useful context sizes and dilute relevance.
Small child chunks are matched for precision, and their larger parent chunks are returned for context.
Smaller chunks reduce context even further.
takeaway: Precise matching + broader context → hierarchical (parent/child) chunking.

question: Customer support articles in a knowledge base vary in length and often switch topics mid-article. Fixed-size chunks sometimes cut a solution in half. Which chunking strategy keeps related sentences together?
options: Default chunking with the maximum overlap
Fixed-size chunking with a 20-token chunk size
Semantic chunking
No chunking
explanations: Overlap helps a little, but boundaries still ignore meaning.
Very small fixed chunks split ideas apart even more often.
Semantic chunking splits text where the meaning changes, so related sentences stay together.
Whole articles mix several topics in one vector.
takeaway: Chunk boundaries that follow meaning → semantic chunking.

question: A company’s knowledge base contains HR policies for several countries. Employees in Germany sometimes receive answers based on the US policy. The team wants retrieval to consider only documents for the employee’s country. What should the team do?
options: Tag documents with country and filter on it
Switch to no chunking so that each policy document is a single chunk
Use a larger foundation model so that it can work out which country’s policy applies
Increase the number of retrieved results
explanations: Metadata filters restrict retrieval to documents that match the attribute.
Chunking changes don’t tell retrieval which country a document belongs to.
The problem is retrieval, not generation quality.
Retrieving more chunks adds more wrong-country documents.
takeaway: Restrict retrieval to a subset of documents → metadata + query-time filters.

question: A bank wants to use call transcripts stored in Amazon S3 to fine-tune a model. Names, account numbers, and addresses in the transcripts must be replaced with placeholders before training. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?
options: Use Amazon Macie to delete the files that contain PII
Run an Amazon Comprehend PII redaction job on the transcripts in S3
Train a custom named entity recognition model on SageMaker AI
Encrypt the transcripts with AWS KMS
explanations: Macie finds sensitive data; deleting files loses the training data instead of redacting it.
Comprehend detects PII entities in text and can produce redacted copies of documents in S3.
Building a custom model takes far more effort than using managed PII detection.
Encryption protects data at rest but leaves PII in the training text.
takeaway: Redact PII in text before training → Comprehend PII detection/redaction.

question: A data lake in Amazon S3 holds thousands of CSV files from different teams. Before the data is used for training, the ML team must find which buckets and files contain sensitive data and mask those columns during ETL. Which TWO services should the team use? (Select TWO.)
options: AWS Glue with the Detect PII transform to mask the columns during ETL
Amazon Inspector to scan the S3 buckets for sensitive data in CSV files
Amazon GuardDuty S3 Protection to find which files contain personal data
Amazon Macie to discover sensitive data across the S3 buckets
AWS Config rules to redact sensitive columns when files are written
explanations: Glue can detect sensitive data in columns and mask or hash it as part of a job.
Inspector finds software vulnerabilities; Macie discovers sensitive data.
GuardDuty S3 Protection detects suspicious access to S3, not sensitive data inside files.
Macie scans S3 objects and reports where sensitive data such as PII is stored.
Config evaluates resource configurations; it doesn’t read or redact file contents.
takeaway: Find sensitive data in S3 → Macie; mask it in pipelines → Glue Detect PII (or Comprehend for free text).

question: An ML engineer is preparing data to fine-tune a text model in Amazon Bedrock so that it writes product descriptions in the company’s style. The engineer has 5,000 examples of product specifications and approved descriptions. How should the training data be prepared?
options: As a CSV file with one row per product description and no inputs
JSONL prompt–completion pairs in S3
As a folder of PDF product sheets in S3 with the approved descriptions on each page
As an Amazon DynamoDB table referenced in the job
explanations: Supervised fine-tuning needs input and output pairs, not just outputs.
Bedrock supervised fine-tuning reads labeled prompt and response pairs in JSONL from S3.
PDFs suit knowledge base ingestion, not supervised fine-tuning.
Customization jobs read training files from S3.
takeaway: Supervised fine-tuning → labeled prompt/completion pairs in JSONL in S3.

question: A pharmaceutical company wants a foundation model to become familiar with its internal research vocabulary. It has millions of unlabeled research reports but very few question-and-answer examples. Which customization approach and data match this situation?
options: Distillation with the reports as teacher responses
Continued pre-training on the unlabeled reports
Supervised fine-tuning with the reports as completions and empty prompts
Reinforcement fine-tuning with the reports as reward functions
explanations: Distillation uses a teacher model to generate responses to prompts; it doesn’t learn from raw documents.
Continued pre-training adapts a model to a domain by training on large volumes of unlabeled text.
Fine-tuning needs task-specific labeled pairs, which the company lacks.
Reward functions score responses; documents can’t serve as rewards.
takeaway: Large unlabeled domain text → continued pre-training; labeled pairs → fine-tuning.

question: A company runs a large foundation model in Amazon Bedrock for a classification-style chatbot and wants a smaller, cheaper model with similar accuracy. It doesn’t have labeled responses but has logged thousands of real user prompts. How should the ML engineer prepare data for Bedrock model distillation?
options: Supply the logged prompts as input
Provide the teacher model’s weights in Amazon S3 so that Bedrock can copy its knowledge
Provide a reward function written in AWS Lambda
Provide labeled responses written by human experts for every prompt
explanations: Distillation needs use-case prompts; Bedrock synthesizes responses from the teacher and trains the student.
Bedrock manages the teacher model; customers don’t supply its weights.
Reward functions are used for reinforcement fine-tuning, not distillation.
Labeled responses are optional for distillation.
takeaway: Distillation → supply prompts (or invocation logs); the teacher generates the training responses.

question: An AWS Glue ETL job loads daily data that is used to retrain a model. Last month, a source system sent a file with 40% null values in a key column, and the retrained model degraded. The team wants the job to evaluate rules and stop bad data from reaching the training dataset. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST effort?
options: Write a custom AWS Lambda function that samples 1% of the rows after each job run finishes
Enable job bookmarks on the Glue job
Add an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the Glue job duration
Glue Data Quality rules that fail the job
explanations: Custom sampling code is more effort and runs after the data is already loaded.
Bookmarks track processed files; they don’t check quality.
Duration doesn’t reveal data content problems.
Glue Data Quality evaluates DQDL rules inside the job and can stop or route bad data.
takeaway: Rule-based quality checks inside ETL → AWS Glue Data Quality.

question: Before building features, an analyst wants statistics for each column of a new dataset, such as missing values, distinct counts, distributions, and correlations, without writing code. Which option should the analyst use?
options: An Amazon Athena CREATE TABLE AS SELECT query
AWS Glue job bookmarks
Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights
An AWS Glue DataBrew profile job on the dataset
explanations: CTAS creates a new table; it doesn’t produce a column profile.
Bookmarks track processed data.
Logs Insights queries log data, not datasets.
DataBrew profile jobs generate column statistics, distributions, and correlations visually.
takeaway: Column-level statistics without code → DataBrew profile job (or the Data Wrangler data quality report).

question: A credit card fraud dataset has 0.3% positive examples. A model trained on it reaches 99.7% accuracy but misses most fraud. Which TWO actions should the ML engineer take? (Select TWO.)
options: Remove the fraud examples that look like normal transactions
Rebalance the validation and test sets to 50% fraud so they match the resampled training data
Report accuracy averaged over 10 cross-validation folds to get a more reliable estimate
Oversample the minority class, for example with SMOTE, or undersample the majority class
Evaluate with recall, precision, and PR AUC
explanations: This discards hard positive examples the model needs.
Evaluation data should keep the real class mix, or the metrics won’t reflect production.
Averaging accuracy doesn’t fix it: accuracy stays near 99.7% even when the model misses fraud.
Rebalancing gives the model enough fraud examples to learn from.
Accuracy hides poor minority-class performance; precision and recall expose it.
takeaway: Imbalanced classes → resample (train only) and judge with precision/recall/PR-AUC, not accuracy.

question: An image classification dataset for detecting defects has 20,000 images of good parts and 600 images of defective parts. Which approach will MOST improve the model’s ability to detect defects?
options: Remove the defective images that look similar so that the class has less redundancy
Augment the defect images
Reduce the image resolution for all images
Convert all images to grayscale
explanations: This shrinks the minority class and makes the imbalance worse.
Augmentation creates realistic variations of the minority class.
Lower resolution can hide small defects.
Color conversion doesn’t address the imbalance.
takeaway: Minority image class → data augmentation of that class.

question: A dataset for a rare disease classifier has 4% positive cases. The ML engineer randomly splits the data into training, validation, and test sets, and finds the validation set has almost no positive cases. Which splitting method should the engineer use?
options: Duplicating positive cases in the validation set
A stratified split on the label
A larger training set and a smaller validation set
A split by row order without shuffling
explanations: Duplicates inflate metrics and don’t represent real data.
Stratification keeps the class proportions the same in each split.
A smaller validation set will have even fewer positives.
Row order may cluster cases and make the imbalance worse.
takeaway: Keep class ratios in every split → stratified splitting.

question: An ML engineer builds a model that predicts next week’s product demand from historical sales. Validation scores are excellent, but the model performs poorly in production. The engineer shuffled all rows before splitting into training and validation sets. What is the MOST likely cause, and what should the engineer do?
options: The learning rate is too high; reduce it
The model underfits; add more features
Future data leaked into training; split the data chronologically
The validation set is too small; increase it to 50%
explanations: Learning rate doesn’t explain good validation but poor production results.
Excellent validation scores don’t indicate underfitting.
For time series, training must use only past data, and validation must use later periods.
Size isn’t the issue; the split leaks future information.
takeaway: Time-dependent data → chronological splits, never random shuffles across time.

question: Before training a loan approval model, an ML engineer must check whether applicants over 60 are underrepresented in the training data compared with other applicants, and whether their historical approval rate differs. Which TWO pre-training bias metrics measure these? (Select TWO.)
options: Disparate impact (DI) of the model’s predictions
Class imbalance (CI) for the age facet
Root mean squared error (RMSE)
Area under the ROC curve (AUC)
Difference in proportions of labels (DPL)
explanations: DI is a post-training metric computed on predictions.
CI measures whether one facet has far fewer examples than another.
RMSE measures regression error, not bias.
AUC measures overall classification performance, not differences between groups.
DPL compares the share of positive labels (approvals) between facets in the training data.
takeaway: Pre-training bias: CI (representation) and DPL (label rates). Post-training: DI, DPPL, and others.

question: A team is preparing an image dataset for a face-based age estimation model. It wants to find out whether some skin tones and age groups are underrepresented before training. What should the team do FIRST?
options: Convert all images to grayscale to remove skin tone information
Increase the image resolution
Measure each group’s share of images
Train the model first and compare its accuracy on the full combined test set
explanations: Removing information doesn’t fix underrepresentation and can hurt accuracy.
Resolution doesn’t change group representation.
Measuring the distribution across groups reveals representation gaps before training.
An aggregate metric can hide poor performance on underrepresented groups.
takeaway: Bias in image or text data starts with measuring how groups are represented.

question: An ML engineer has 20,000 prompt-response pairs collected from employees to fine-tune a model. Some pairs are duplicates, some have empty responses, and a few contain offensive language. Which TWO steps should the engineer take before starting the fine-tuning job? (Select TWO.)
options: Increase the number of epochs so that the model can ignore bad examples
Convert the dataset from JSONL to CSV so that the fine-tuning job reads it faster
Remove duplicates and pairs with empty or truncated fields
Screen the pairs with the Bedrock Guardrails ApplyGuardrail API and remove flagged pairs
Keep every pair and add a system prompt during fine-tuning that tells the model to ignore offensive text
explanations: More epochs make the model memorize bad examples.
Bedrock fine-tuning expects JSONL, and the format doesn’t fix duplicates or harmful content.
Structural checks and deduplication keep invalid or repeated examples out of training.
ApplyGuardrail evaluates any text against content filters without invoking a model.
The model learns from every pair it sees; bad examples must be removed, not explained away.
takeaway: Fine-tuning data integrity → schema and duplicate checks plus content safety screening.

question: A dataset of server metrics used to train a capacity model contains rare extreme spikes caused by logging errors. The team wants an unsupervised SageMaker AI built-in algorithm to score each record by how anomalous it is so they can review and remove the errors. Which algorithm should they use?
options: DeepAR
Random Cut Forest (RCF), the anomaly scoring algorithm
BlazingText
Linear Learner in binary classification mode
explanations: DeepAR forecasts time series; it doesn’t score anomalies for cleaning.
RCF is an unsupervised algorithm that assigns an anomaly score to each data point.
BlazingText is for text classification and word embeddings.
Linear Learner is supervised and needs labeled anomalies.
takeaway: Unsupervised anomaly scores → Random Cut Forest.

question: A numeric feature for household income has 8% missing values and a long right tail of very high incomes. Which imputation approach is MOST appropriate?
options: Replace missing values with the median, plus a missing-value flag
Drop the income feature because it has missing values
Replace missing values with zero to mark them as unknown
Replace missing values with the mean income of all customers
explanations: The median resists outliers, and a missing-value flag lets the model learn from the pattern of missingness.
The feature is 92% complete and likely useful.
Zero income is a real value and would bias the feature.
The mean is pulled up by the long tail and misrepresents typical values.
takeaway: Skewed numeric with missing values → median imputation (plus an indicator).

question: A text classification model scores 98% on the test set but 81% in production. The ML engineer finds that many support tickets were submitted twice with identical text and that the duplicates were split randomly. What should the engineer do?
options: Deduplicate before splitting
Train for fewer epochs
Add dropout and L2 regularization to the model so that it memorizes less text
Increase the size of the test set
explanations: Duplicates across splits leak answers into evaluation and inflate test scores.
Fewer epochs don’t remove the leaked duplicates.
Regularization doesn’t fix contaminated evaluation data.
More data with the same leakage still inflates scores.
takeaway: Deduplicate before splitting to avoid train/test leakage.

question: A model predicts whether a customer will cancel a subscription next month. It performs suspiciously well in validation. Which TWO features are MOST likely to cause target leakage and should be removed? (Select TWO.)
options: cancellation_reason, which is filled in when the customer cancels
final_invoice_date, which is set when an account closes
number_of_support_tickets in the last 90 days
days_since_last_login, calculated from activity before the prediction date
plan_type at the time of prediction
explanations: This value exists only after the outcome happens, so it leaks the label.
It’s created by the cancellation itself and won’t be known at prediction time.
Past tickets are known at prediction time.
This is known before the prediction is made, so it is a legitimate feature.
The current plan is known before the outcome.
takeaway: Leakage: features that are only known after (or because of) the outcome.

question: Several data scientists share Python feature engineering libraries and intermediate datasets of about 200 GB across SageMaker Studio and EC2-based processing scripts. They need a POSIX file system that multiple instances can mount at the same time. Which storage option should they use?
options: Amazon EFS
Instance store volumes
Amazon EBS gp3 volumes
Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
explanations: EFS is a shared, elastic POSIX file system that many instances can mount concurrently.
Instance store is local to one instance and is lost when it stops.
An EBS volume is typically attached to one instance at a time.
Archive storage requires restores and isn’t a mounted file system.
takeaway: Shared POSIX file system across instances → Amazon EFS.

question: A data lake in Amazon S3 is cataloged in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. ML engineers in the fraud team must query only some columns of a customer table with Athena, and must not see the date_of_birth and address columns. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Create a separate S3 copy of the table without the restricted columns
Use S3 bucket policies to deny access to specific columns
Use AWS Lake Formation column-level permissions on the Data Catalog table
Encrypt the restricted columns with a different KMS key
explanations: Copies must be kept in sync and add storage and pipeline work.
Bucket policies work at the object level and can’t hide columns.
Lake Formation grants fine-grained column, row, and cell-level access that Athena enforces.
Encryption doesn’t provide column-level access control in Athena queries.
takeaway: Column- or row-level access to data lake tables → Lake Formation fine-grained permissions.

question: An ML engineer is joining a 3 TB clickstream dataset with a 2 GB product catalog in an AWS Glue PySpark job. The join causes heavy shuffling and slow runs. Which change will MOST improve performance?
options: Repartition the clickstream data into a single partition
Broadcast the small product catalog to every executor (a broadcast join)
Run the join in a Python shell job instead
Convert the clickstream data to CSV before the join
explanations: One partition removes parallelism and can cause memory failures.
Broadcasting the small table avoids shuffling the large dataset across the cluster.
A single-node Python shell job can’t handle 3 TB efficiently.
CSV is slower to read than columnar formats and doesn’t reduce shuffling.
takeaway: Large table joined with a small one in Spark → broadcast join.

question: A company wants to build a RAG assistant over PDF manuals that contain tables, charts, and scanned pages. Default text extraction loses the table structure. What should the ML engineer configure when creating the Amazon Bedrock knowledge base data source?
options: A smaller fixed chunk size with no overlap between the chunks
Advanced parsing (Bedrock Data Automation or an FM parser)
A larger embedding model with more output dimensions per chunk
Metadata filters that exclude scanned pages and image-heavy files
explanations: Chunk size doesn’t recover table structure lost during parsing.
Advanced parsing extracts tables, figures, and scanned text from complex documents before chunking.
Embeddings can’t restore content that parsing dropped.
Filters restrict retrieval; they don’t improve extraction.
takeaway: Complex PDFs with tables or images → advanced parsing (BDA or FM parser) in the knowledge base.

question: An ML engineer needs a nightly extract of several large tables from an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL production database for feature engineering. Heavy analytical queries must not slow down the application. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
options: Run the extract from a read replica of the database
Increase the primary instance size and run the queries on it at midnight
Enable Multi-AZ and query the standby instance
Run the extract queries against the primary instance during business hours
explanations: A read replica serves read-heavy extract queries without loading the primary.
A bigger primary costs more and still shares resources with the application.
The Multi-AZ standby isn’t readable in a standard Multi-AZ deployment.
Analytical scans on the primary compete with application traffic.
takeaway: Offload analytical reads from production → read replica (or snapshot export to S3).

question: A company already publishes payment events to an Apache Kafka cluster that it manages. The ML team needs per-merchant aggregates over 10-minute windows, computed continuously and written to a feature store. Which AWS service should process the Kafka stream?
options: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink
Amazon Data Firehose with a 10-minute buffer
Amazon Athena with scheduled queries
AWS Glue DataBrew recipe jobs
explanations: Flink reads from Kafka and Kinesis sources and computes stateful windowed aggregations continuously.
Firehose buffers and delivers records; it doesn’t compute per-key aggregates.
Scheduled batch SQL can’t keep windowed features continuously up to date.
DataBrew runs batch jobs on datasets, not on live streams.
takeaway: Windowed aggregations over Kafka or Kinesis → Managed Service for Apache Flink.

question: Which AWS service delivers streaming records to Amazon S3 in near real time with automatic scaling, buffering, and no consumer code to write?
options: AWS Batch
Amazon Data Firehose delivery streams
Amazon SQS
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams
explanations: Batch runs containerized batch jobs.
Firehose is a managed delivery service that buffers and writes streaming data to destinations such as S3.
SQS queues messages for consumers to process; it doesn’t deliver files to S3.
Data Streams stores the stream, but you must write or configure consumers.
takeaway: Near-real-time delivery to S3 without code → Data Firehose.

question: A streaming pipeline writes events to Amazon S3 for model training. Producers add new optional fields every few weeks, and downstream jobs break when the schema changes. The team wants a compact, schema-aware row format for the raw landing zone, with columnar files later for analytics. Which format should the raw zone use?
options: CSV with a header row in every file
Microsoft Excel workbooks
Apache Avro files with a registered schema
Plain text logs with one event per line
explanations: CSV has no type information and breaks easily when columns change.
Excel isn’t suited to streaming or large-scale processing.
Avro is a compact row format that stores schemas and supports adding optional fields.
Unstructured text has no schema to evolve.
takeaway: Row-oriented, schema-evolving streams → Avro; analytics copies → Parquet/ORC.

question: An ML engineer creates an Amazon OpenSearch Serverless vector index for a knowledge base and then switches the embedding model from one that outputs 1,024 dimensions to one that outputs 512 dimensions. Ingestion now fails. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: The new model needs Provisioned Throughput before it can embed text
Its vector field is fixed at 1,024 dimensions, which no longer match
The data source must use hierarchical chunking with a 512-dimension model
OpenSearch Serverless doesn’t support vectors with fewer than 1,024 dimensions
explanations: Embedding models run on demand; capacity isn’t the cause of a schema error.
Vector dimensions are fixed when the field is created, so a new model needs a matching index (and re-embedding).
Chunking strategy is unrelated to vector dimensions.
Vector fields support a range of dimensions; the problem is the mismatch.
takeaway: Vector field dimensions must match the embedding model; changing models means re-indexing and re-embedding.

question: A RAG application uses an HNSW vector index. Queries are fast, but evaluation shows that some relevant passages are missed. Which TWO changes will MOST likely improve recall? (Select TWO.)
options: Quantize the vectors to binary to reduce index memory and speed up queries
Lower ef_search at query time so that the graph search returns results sooner
Reduce the number of results returned from 10 to 2
Increase the HNSW search parameter (ef_search) at query time
Rebuild the index with higher m and ef_construction settings
explanations: Aggressive quantization trades recall for memory and speed, the opposite of the goal.
A smaller ef_search explores fewer candidates and lowers recall further.
Returning fewer results lowers the chance that the relevant passage is included.
A larger candidate list during search explores more of the graph and finds more true neighbors.
A denser, better-built graph improves recall at the cost of memory and build time.
takeaway: HNSW: higher ef_search, m, ef_construction → better recall, more cost/latency.

question: A call center wants to train a model that predicts customer churn from what was said on calls. It has 2 years of recorded calls in Amazon S3. What should the ML engineer do FIRST to turn the recordings into model-ready data?
options: Transcribe the calls in batch with PII redaction
Use Amazon Translate to convert the audio files into text
Use Amazon Polly to convert the recordings into speech markups
Use Amazon Rekognition to label the audio files
explanations: Transcripts make the spoken content usable for NLP features, and redaction protects customer data.
Translate converts text between languages; it doesn’t transcribe audio.
Polly turns text into speech, not speech into text.
Rekognition analyzes images and video.
takeaway: Speech recordings → Transcribe (with PII redaction) → text features.

question: Three teams compute the same customer features with different code, and models behave differently in training and in production because the feature logic differs. Which approach will MOST reduce this problem?
options: Store the features in each model’s container image
Define features once in Feature Store; all teams read them
Ask each team to document its feature code in a wiki
Have each team recompute features nightly in separate S3 buckets
explanations: Baking features into images duplicates logic and gets stale.
A shared feature store gives one definition, consistent offline and online values, and discovery across teams.
Documentation doesn’t stop the implementations from drifting apart.
Separate pipelines keep the inconsistency.
takeaway: Consistent, reusable features for training and serving → Feature Store.

question: A recommendation model reads session features from the SageMaker AI Feature Store online store. Records for inactive sessions should disappear automatically after 24 hours to keep the online store small. What should the ML engineer configure?
options: A daily batch transform job that deletes old records
An S3 Lifecycle rule on the offline store prefix
A smaller instance type for the online store
A time to live (TTL) duration on the online store records
explanations: Custom deletion jobs add work that TTL already handles.
Lifecycle rules affect the offline store files in S3, not online records.
The online store is managed; there’s no instance to size.
TTL expires online records automatically after the configured duration.
takeaway: Auto-expire stale online features → online store TTL.

question: Clickstream records delivered by Amazon Data Firehose must have a hashed user ID and an added product category before they land in S3. The logic is simple and stateless. Which solution requires the LEAST additional infrastructure?
options: An Amazon EMR cluster that reads from Firehose
A SageMaker AI processing job that runs every minute
A Lambda transformation on the Firehose stream
An AWS Glue crawler that rewrites the records
explanations: Firehose doesn’t feed EMR clusters, and a cluster is heavy for simple logic.
Frequent batch jobs add cost and complexity for per-record logic.
Firehose invokes a Lambda function on buffered records and delivers the transformed output.
Crawlers infer schemas; they don’t transform records.
takeaway: Simple per-record changes in delivery → Firehose Lambda transformation.

question: A fraud model uses a merchant_id feature with 400,000 distinct values. One-hot encoding makes the training data enormous and slow to train. Which TWO encoding approaches are MOST appropriate? (Select TWO.)
options: Label encoding the IDs as 1 to 400,000 for a linear model
Feature hashing into a fixed number of buckets
Dropping merchant_id and keeping the merchant name text
One-hot encoding with a larger instance type
Target encoding computed on the training folds only
explanations: Arbitrary integers imply an order and distance that don’t exist.
Hashing maps many categories into a fixed-width vector with no lookup table.
The name has the same cardinality problem and loses the ID signal.
More memory doesn’t fix the dimensional explosion.
Replacing each ID with a smoothed target statistic keeps one column; computing it on training data avoids leakage.
takeaway: High-cardinality categories → target encoding (leak-safe) or feature hashing; embeddings for deep models.

question: A numeric feature has a few extreme outliers. After min-max normalization, almost all values are squeezed into a tiny range near 0. The model is sensitive to feature scale. What should the ML engineer do?
options: Multiply every value by 1,000
Use a robust or standard scaler and handle the outliers
One-hot encode the feature
Apply min-max normalization a second time to spread the values
explanations: A constant factor keeps the same relative squeeze.
Standardization or median/IQR-based scaling is less distorted by extremes, especially after capping or log-transforming outliers.
One-hot encoding is for categorical values.
Normalizing again doesn’t change the squeezed distribution.
takeaway: Outliers squash min-max scaling → robust scaling or standardization plus outlier handling.

topic: One embedding model for both sides
question: A team embeds its documents with one embedding model and, to save cost, embeds user queries with a different, cheaper model. Retrieval quality is very poor. Why?
options: The cheaper model outputs more dimensions than the document model
Queries need a multimodal embedding model, even for plain text search
Their vectors live in different spaces, so scores mean nothing
Documents must be embedded twice
explanations: Dimension count isn’t the main issue.
Text queries can use a text embedding model.
Queries and documents must be embedded with the same model for comparisons to work.
Double embedding doesn’t fix mismatched spaces.
takeaway: Use the same embedding model (and version) for documents and queries.

question: An ML engineer embeds long contracts with an embedding model that accepts up to 8,000 tokens per input. Contracts of 30,000 tokens produce embeddings that ignore most of the text. What should the engineer do?
options: Compress each contract into a ZIP file before sending it to the model
Embed the title and first page of each contract instead
Chunk each contract within the token limit and embed the chunks
Increase the embedding model’s temperature
explanations: Compression doesn’t change the token limit.
Titles and first pages lose most of the content.
Chunking keeps all content within the model’s input limit and improves retrieval granularity.
Embedding models don’t use temperature.
takeaway: Inputs beyond the embedding model’s limit are truncated → chunk first.

question: With fixed-size chunking, answers sometimes miss information because a key sentence is split between two chunks. Which setting helps the MOST?
options: Add overlap between consecutive chunks
Use a larger generation model for the answers
Remove metadata from the documents
Lower the number of retrieved chunks
explanations: Overlap repeats boundary text in both chunks, so sentences near the edges stay intact in at least one.
Generation can’t recover text that retrieval split apart.
Metadata doesn’t cause split sentences.
Retrieving less makes missing context more likely.
takeaway: Boundary splits → chunk overlap (or semantic/hierarchical chunking).

question: Data scientists must join customer tables from three systems by email address, but they must never see the actual addresses. The analytics team wants the joins to keep working. Which technique should the data pipeline apply to the email column?
options: Redact the email column by deleting it
Consistent keyed hashing
Mask each email as ****@****
Encrypt the column with a different random key in each system
explanations: Removing the column breaks the joins.
A consistent keyed hash produces the same token for the same email, so joins work without exposing the value.
Identical masks for every row make joins impossible.
Different keys produce different values, which breaks joins.
takeaway: Need joins without raw values → consistent keyed hashing (pseudonymization).

question: An ML engineer is fine-tuning a model in Amazon Bedrock with 6,000 prompt-completion pairs. The engineer wants to detect overfitting during the job. What should the engineer provide?
options: Just the training data, with more epochs to compensate
The separate test set, used during training for early stopping decisions
A held-out validation dataset, for example 10–20% of the pairs
The same 6,000 pairs as both training and validation data
explanations: More epochs without validation hides overfitting.
The test set should stay untouched for the final evaluation.
Validation loss during training shows when the model starts to overfit.
Identical data can’t reveal overfitting.
takeaway: Customization jobs: provide a held-out validation set and keep a separate test set.

question: A team wants to improve a model’s ability to write SQL queries that return correct results. It can automatically check whether a generated query runs and returns the expected rows, but it has few hand-written reference queries. Which TWO items should the team prepare for reinforcement fine-tuning in Amazon Bedrock? (Select TWO.)
options: A knowledge base of SQL documentation
A dataset of representative prompts (or existing invocation logs)
A reward function, for example in AWS Lambda, that scores each generated query
Millions of unlabeled database documents for continued pre-training
A teacher model’s responses for distilling into a smaller student model
explanations: A knowledge base supports RAG, not reinforcement fine-tuning.
Reinforcement fine-tuning learns from responses to your prompts.
The reward function provides the feedback signal instead of labeled answers.
That prepares data for continued pre-training, not reinforcement fine-tuning.
That is the input for model distillation, not reinforcement fine-tuning with a reward function.
takeaway: RFT = prompts + reward function (graders), not labeled answers.

question: A team has a new dataset in the AWS Glue Data Catalog and doesn’t know which data quality rules to write. Which feature helps it get started fastest?
options: AWS Glue Data Quality rule recommendations
AWS Glue job bookmarks on the dataset
AWS Glue crawler schedules that rescan the table
Amazon Athena workgroups with query limits
explanations: Glue Data Quality analyzes the data and suggests DQDL rules that you can review and apply.
Bookmarks track processed data.
Schedules control when crawlers run.
Workgroups manage query settings and costs.
takeaway: Starting point for quality rules → Glue Data Quality recommendations.

question: A team is labeling 50,000 medical images with a small group of annotators. Spot checks show inconsistent labels between annotators. Which TWO practices will MOST improve label quality? (Select TWO.)
options: Drop every image that annotators disagree on and keep the unanimous ones
Write clear labeling instructions with examples of edge cases
Let each annotator choose their own label names
Train the model first and keep the labels for images it gets right
Have multiple annotators label each image and use consensus or review for disagreements
explanations: Hard, ambiguous cases are often the most valuable; resolve them with review instead of discarding them.
Clear guidelines reduce disagreement between annotators.
Inconsistent label names make the data unusable.
This biases the dataset toward easy cases.
Consensus labeling catches individual mistakes and flags ambiguous items.
takeaway: Label quality → clear guidelines + multiple annotators with consensus/review.

question: A company must label 2 million support tickets by topic. Human labeling of every ticket is too expensive. Which approach reduces cost while keeping quality?
options: Label a random 1% and assume the rest match
Use the ticket length as the label
Model pre-labels; humans review low-confidence items
Ask a foundation model to label everything with no review
explanations: Unlabeled data can’t be used for supervised training.
Length isn’t a topic label.
Pre-labeling with human review of uncertain items (active-learning style) cuts cost while catching errors.
Unreviewed model labels can contain systematic errors.
takeaway: Cheaper labeling → model pre-labels + humans review uncertain items.

question: A team that already uses Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth for image labeling wants to reduce the number of images that human workers must label for a new 100,000-image job. Which feature should the team enable?
options: Feature Store online store
Model Registry approval
Debugger built-in rules
Automated data labeling
explanations: Feature Store serves features.
Model Registry manages model versions.
Debugger monitors training jobs.
Automated labeling trains a model on human labels and labels high-confidence items automatically, sending the rest to humans.
takeaway: Ground Truth automated labeling = active learning. (Ground Truth is closed to new customers since July 2026; existing users keep it.)

question: A model predicts patient readmission from hospital visits. Each patient has many visits, and the visits were split randomly into training and test sets. Test performance is much higher than performance on new patients. What should the ML engineer do?
options: Split by patient
Use a larger test set
Stratify the split by readmission label
Shuffle the visits again before splitting them randomly
explanations: A group-based split prevents the model from memorizing patients that also appear in the test set.
More data with the same leakage still inflates the score.
Stratification balances labels but still puts the same patient in both sets.
Shuffling again doesn’t keep patients together.
takeaway: Repeated entities → group-based splits (by customer, patient, device).

question: Training data for a non-time-series classifier is stored sorted by label: all negatives first, then all positives. Training with mini-batches converges poorly. What should the ML engineer do?
options: Sort the data by label in the opposite order
Increase the batch size to 1
Remove half of the negative examples
Shuffle the training data before each training run
explanations: Any label ordering creates biased mini-batches.
A batch size of 1 makes training noisier.
Undersampling doesn’t fix the ordering problem.
Shuffling mixes classes in every mini-batch so gradients reflect the whole dataset.
takeaway: Independent rows sorted by label → shuffle before training.

question: A team is building a resume screening model from historical hiring data. It wants to find bias in the text data before training. Which TWO checks are MOST useful? (Select TWO.)
options: Compare the share of examples and positive labels across demographic groups
Count spelling errors in each resume
Compare model accuracy on a held-out test set after training to see whether bias exists
Remove the name and gender fields, then treat the remaining resume text as free of bias
Search the text for proxy terms, such as gendered words, that correlate with protected attributes
explanations: Representation and label-rate differences (CI and DPL) reveal historical bias in the data.
Spelling errors aren’t a bias measure.
Overall accuracy doesn’t reveal group differences, and this check comes after training.
Proxy terms in the text can still encode protected attributes.
Proxy features let a model learn protected attributes indirectly.
takeaway: Text bias: group representation and label rates, plus proxy terms.

question: An ML engineer trains the SageMaker AI built-in XGBoost algorithm on data with 2% positive examples. The engineer wants the model to pay more attention to positives without changing the dataset. Which hyperparameter should the engineer set?
options: colsample_bytree
min_child_weight
num_round
scale_pos_weight
explanations: colsample_bytree samples features for each tree.
min_child_weight controls the minimum weight needed to split a node.
num_round sets the number of boosting rounds.
scale_pos_weight increases the weight of positive examples, a common setting is negatives ÷ positives.
takeaway: Imbalance in XGBoost without resampling → scale_pos_weight.

question: A team fine-tunes a model on customer support conversations and then evaluates it on a public benchmark and its own test questions. The scores are surprisingly high. The team learns that some test questions were copied into the fine-tuning data. What should the team do?
options: Remove test items from the training data and re-evaluate
Fine-tune for fewer epochs
Add more test questions from the same public benchmark set
Switch to a larger base model
explanations: Removing overlap between training and test data restores an honest measure of quality.
Fewer epochs don’t remove the contamination.
More contaminated questions still inflate scores.
A larger model doesn’t fix contaminated evaluation data.
takeaway: Keep evaluation data out of training data; deduplicate across splits.

question: A company collected 50,000 public forum posts to fine-tune a customer-facing model. Some posts contain hate speech and personal information. Which approach should the ML engineer use to screen the data at scale with the LEAST custom code?
options: Train the model first and filter its outputs later
Use Amazon Translate to translate the posts
Have two reviewers read every post manually before training
Screen posts with ApplyGuardrail, then drop or mask flagged ones
explanations: Harmful training data can shape the model’s behavior.
Translation doesn’t remove harmful content.
Manual review of 50,000 posts is slow and costly.
ApplyGuardrail checks text against content and PII filters without invoking a model.
takeaway: Screen training text at scale → ApplyGuardrail (content + PII filters).

question: A training dataset was assembled from several exports, and about 12% of rows are exact duplicates. Which problem is this MOST likely to cause?
options: Over-weighted repeats and train/test leakage
Training jobs fail with an out-of-memory error
Feature scaling no longer works on the duplicated columns
The model can’t be deployed to an endpoint
explanations: Duplicates bias training toward repeated rows and can appear in both splits, inflating scores.
A 12% increase rarely causes memory failures.
Scaling still works with duplicates.
Duplicates don’t affect deployment.
takeaway: Deduplicate before splitting and training.

question: An ML engineer wants a simple, explainable rule to flag outliers in a numeric feature before training. Which approach is common and easy to explain?
options: Flag values outside Q1 − 1.5×IQR and Q3 + 1.5×IQR
Flag values with more than two decimal places
Flag values that appear a single time in the dataset
Flag every value above the mean
explanations: The interquartile range rule is a simple, robust outlier test.
Precision isn’t related to outliers.
Uniqueness doesn’t indicate an outlier in continuous data.
Half the data would be flagged.
takeaway: Simple outlier rule → IQR fences; unsupervised scoring → Random Cut Forest.

question: A categorical feature, preferred_channel, is missing for 15% of customers, and missingness itself may be informative. What is a good way to handle it?
options: Delete all rows with missing values
Replace missing values with randomly chosen categories
Add an explicit “unknown” category for the missing values
Replace missing values with the mean
explanations: Dropping 15% of rows wastes data and can bias the sample.
Random values add noise.
An explicit category keeps the rows and lets the model learn from missingness.
A mean doesn’t exist for categories.
takeaway: Missing categories → an explicit “unknown” category (or mode, if missingness isn’t informative).

question: A European bank must keep customer training data in the EU and prove that it can’t be copied to other Regions by mistake. Which TWO controls help meet this requirement? (Select TWO.)
options: Store the data in S3 buckets in an EU Region
Use global cross-Region inference for all models
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration
Use an SCP that denies actions outside approved EU Regions
Turn on SSE-S3 default encryption for each bucket
explanations: Data stored in an EU Region stays there unless someone copies it.
Global profiles can route requests to any Region worldwide.
Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads; it doesn’t restrict Regions.
A service control policy prevents creating resources or copying data to other Regions.
Encryption protects the data but doesn’t control which Region it is stored in.
takeaway: Residency → store in-Region + SCP Region guardrails (and geographic, not global, inference profiles).

question: Raw training data older than 1 year is rarely used but must be kept for 7 years for audits. Which approach MOST reduces storage cost automatically?
options: A Lifecycle rule to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 1 year
Copy the data to Amazon EBS snapshots for long-term storage
Delete data older than 1 year to save storage costs
Keep everything in S3 Standard for fast audits
explanations: Lifecycle rules move cold data to the cheapest archive class automatically.
Snapshots are for volumes and cost more than archive storage.
The audit requirement needs the data for 7 years.
Standard is the most expensive class for rarely accessed data.
takeaway: Rarely used, must keep → Lifecycle transition to Glacier classes.

question: A training job fails because some input objects are in the S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval storage class. What must happen before the job can read them?
options: The execution role needs glacier:ReadObject permission
The bucket must have Transfer Acceleration enabled
Restore the objects (or copy them to another class) first
The training job must switch to Pipe input mode to read them
explanations: Permissions don’t replace the restore step.
Acceleration doesn’t restore objects.
Objects in Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive need a restore request before they can be read.
Input modes can’t read objects that need a restore.
