takeaway: Glacier Flexible Retrieval/Deep Archive objects must be restored before use.

question: A SageMaker AI training job reads only 10 of 300 columns from a 4 TB dataset in Amazon S3. Which TWO changes will reduce data loading time and cost? (Select TWO.)
options: Create a narrower extract with just the 10 columns, for example with an Athena CTAS query
Copy the full 4 TB dataset to a larger EBS volume before each training run
Store the dataset as Parquet so jobs read only the needed columns
Store the dataset as one large uncompressed CSV file
Turn on S3 Transfer Acceleration for the bucket that holds the dataset
explanations: A smaller extract means less data to move into training.
Copying all 300 columns adds time and storage cost instead of reducing them.
Columnar files let readers skip unneeded columns.
Uncompressed CSV is the slowest and largest option.
Transfer Acceleration speeds up long-distance transfers; the job still reads all 300 columns.
takeaway: Read less data → columnar formats and narrow extracts.

question: An ML engineer joins an orders table with a customers table in a Glue job. The output has more rows than the orders table, and order totals are inflated. What is the MOST likely cause?
options: The orders table is stored as Parquet
Duplicate customer IDs, so orders match several rows
Job bookmarks were enabled
The Glue job used too few workers to complete the join
explanations: File format doesn’t change join semantics.
Duplicate keys on one side of a join multiply rows on the other side.
Bookmarks affect which files are read, not join multiplicity.
Worker count doesn’t change join results.
takeaway: Row explosion after a join → duplicate keys; deduplicate dimension tables first.

topic: Choose a vector store for existing apps
question: A team already runs Amazon OpenSearch Service for log search and wants vector search for a new RAG feature with metadata filtering and low-latency queries at thousands of requests per second. Which option fits BEST?
options: Amazon S3 Vectors for all queries
Amazon Redshift materialized views of the embeddings
k-NN vector indexes in OpenSearch Service
Amazon DynamoDB global secondary indexes
explanations: S3 Vectors suits large, infrequently queried sets, not thousands of queries per second.
Redshift isn’t designed for low-latency vector search.
OpenSearch handles high-throughput, low-latency vector search with filtering, and the team already runs it.
GSIs provide key lookups, not similarity search.
takeaway: High QPS, low latency, filters → OpenSearch k-NN; cheap and cold → S3 Vectors.

question: A team stores 5 million training images. Which storage service is the MOST appropriate default for this data?
options: Amazon EBS
Amazon ElastiCache
Amazon DynamoDB
Amazon S3
explanations: EBS volumes attach to individual instances.
In-memory storage is costly and not durable for datasets.
DynamoDB items are limited to 400 KB.
S3 is durable, scalable, low-cost object storage that training jobs read directly.
takeaway: Default store for ML datasets → Amazon S3.

question: Lab instruments on premises keep writing files that a nightly training pipeline in AWS must read. The instruments only support writing to an SMB file share, and the team wants the files to land in Amazon S3 automatically. Which service should the team use?
options: Amazon Kinesis Video Streams from each instrument
AWS Storage Gateway S3 File Gateway
AWS DataSync with a one-time task
Amazon EFS mounted on premises
explanations: This is for video streams, not file shares.
S3 File Gateway presents an SMB or NFS share on premises and stores the files as objects in S3.
A one-time transfer doesn’t keep up with ongoing writes.
EFS isn’t presented as an SMB share for these instruments.
takeaway: Ongoing on-prem file writes to S3 via SMB/NFS → S3 File Gateway.

question: A dataset of scanned forms will be used to train a document classifier. Some forms show customers’ handwritten names and ID numbers. Which approach finds this sensitive text so it can be redacted?
options: Textract to read the text, then Comprehend to find PII
Amazon Polly
Amazon Macie scans run directly on the image files in S3
Amazon Translate
explanations: Textract reads printed and handwritten text, and Comprehend finds PII entities in the extracted text.
Polly converts text to speech.
Macie analyzes text-based content in S3 and doesn’t read handwriting in images.
Translate converts text between languages.
takeaway: PII inside scanned images → Textract (OCR) + Comprehend PII.

question: Why do LLM token counts differ from word counts?
options: Each character becomes exactly one token
Punctuation is ignored by every tokenizer
Each token corresponds to a whole sentence
Tokenizers split many words into several subword pieces
explanations: Most tokenizers group characters into pieces.
Punctuation usually becomes tokens.
Tokens are much smaller than sentences.
Subword tokenization breaks uncommon words into multiple tokens.
takeaway: Tokens ≈ subword pieces; cost and limits are in tokens, not words.

question: A medical NLP classifier performs poorly on notes that use abbreviations such as “SOB” and “HTN,” which are rare in the training data. Which approach will MOST improve robustness?
options: Augment with common clinical abbreviations and expansions
Remove all abbreviations from the training data before training
Translate the notes into another language and back
Lowercase all text
explanations: Domain-specific augmentation exposes the model to the variations it will see.
The model would still fail on abbreviations in production.
Generic back-translation can mangle clinical abbreviations.
Lowercasing doesn’t teach the meaning of abbreviations.
takeaway: Domain-specific augmentation (synonyms, abbreviations) improves robustness to real input variation.

question: A legal team wants a knowledge base to filter contracts by client name, contract type, and signing year. Thousands of contracts are PDFs with no metadata. Which approach adds the attributes with the LEAST manual work?
options: Rename the PDF files with random IDs
Extract fields automatically
Ask lawyers to type the metadata for every contract by hand
Increase the chunk size
explanations: Random names don’t create filterable attributes.
Automated extraction creates the metadata used for filtering at query time.
Manual entry for thousands of files is slow.
Chunk size doesn’t create metadata.
takeaway: Metadata for filtering can be extracted automatically during document preparation.

question: A hospital wants an external vendor to prototype a model, but it can’t share real patient records. The vendor needs data with realistic distributions and relationships. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
options: Generate synthetic records with realistic distributions
Share the data encrypted with a key the vendor holds
Share a random sample of 100 real records under an NDA
Share the real data with patient names and addresses removed
explanations: Synthetic data can mimic distributions and correlations without exposing individuals.
The vendor could decrypt and see real data.
Even a small sample exposes real patients.
Removing names alone can still allow re-identification.
takeaway: Prototype without exposing real people → synthetic data (validate it for privacy and fidelity).

question: A weekly retraining pipeline breaks when an upstream team renames a column. The ML engineer wants the pipeline to stop with a clear error before training starts. Which TWO actions help? (Select TWO.)
options: Add a schema and data quality check step, such as Glue Data Quality, before training
Disable validation so the job keeps running
Increase the training job’s maximum run time so slow runs aren’t stopped
Add a retry policy to the training step so the pipeline tries again three times before failing
Agree on a versioned data contract with the upstream team
explanations: An explicit check fails fast with a clear message when expected columns are missing.
Silent failures train models on wrong data.
Longer runs don’t fix missing columns.
Retries repeat the same failure; the renamed column needs to be caught before training.
Contracts and versioning prevent surprise breaking changes.
takeaway: Fail fast on schema drift → explicit validation step + data contracts.

question: A delivery model uses order timestamps from many countries stored in local time without offsets. Features such as hour of day behave inconsistently. What should the ML engineer do?
options: Convert to UTC first
Drop all timestamp features
Round every timestamp to the nearest day
Encode the raw local timestamp strings with one-hot encoding
explanations: Consistent time handling makes derived features comparable.
Time features are often strong predictors.
Rounding loses the hour-of-day signal.
Nearly every timestamp is unique.
takeaway: Inconsistent time zones → normalize to UTC, then derive local features deliberately.

question: A linear model predicts house prices. The effect of size on price is much larger in city centers than in suburbs, and the linear model can’t capture this. Which feature engineering step helps?
options: Add a size × is_city_center interaction feature to the data
Normalize the size feature to the range 0–1
Bin the size feature into two equal-width buckets
Remove the location feature from the model
explanations: Interaction terms let linear models represent effects that depend on another feature.
Scaling doesn’t create interactions.
Coarse binning loses detail and still lacks the interaction.
This removes useful information.
takeaway: Effects that depend on another feature → interaction terms (or a tree model).

question: Before training a CNN, an ML engineer scales pixel values from 0–255 to 0–1 and resizes images to the same dimensions. Why?
options: It removes class imbalance
Amazon S3 requires it before images can be stored
It encrypts the images
Fixed input sizes and scaled pixel values help the network train
explanations: Resizing doesn’t change class counts.
S3 stores images of any size and range.
Scaling isn’t encryption.
Networks need fixed input shapes, and scaled inputs keep gradients well behaved.
takeaway: Image preprocessing: resize + scale pixel values.

question: Auditors ask the ML team to reproduce a model trained 8 months ago, but the training data in S3 has been overwritten several times. Which TWO practices would have made this possible? (Select TWO.)
options: Record the dataset version or URI with each training run, for example in MLflow
Store the data in an instance store volume
Enable S3 Versioning (or write immutable, dated dataset snapshots)
Store the data in S3 Intelligent-Tiering so that older versions move to cheaper tiers
Keep the training code in Git with a tag for every model that goes to production
explanations: Linking runs to data versions makes them reproducible.
Instance store is temporary.
Versioned or immutable datasets keep the exact data used for each run.
Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between access tiers; it doesn’t keep earlier versions of overwritten objects.
Versioned code alone can’t reproduce a model when the data it used is gone.
takeaway: Reproducibility → versioned/immutable data + lineage recorded per run.

question: Customer profile changes are written to an Amazon DynamoDB table. A real-time model needs the latest profile features in the SageMaker AI Feature Store online store within seconds of each change. Which design meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
options: A SageMaker AI processing job that polls the table every minute with Scan
DynamoDB Streams with a Lambda function that calls PutRecord
A nightly AWS Glue job that copies the whole table into the offline store
An hourly Athena query that exports changed rows to Amazon S3 for ingestion
explanations: Polling with Scan is costly, slow, and consumes read capacity.
Streams capture each change, and Lambda writes it to the online store within seconds.
Nightly batch copies are far too slow and update the offline store, not the online store.
Hourly exports miss the seconds-level freshness requirement.
takeaway: Database changes → features in seconds: DynamoDB Streams + Lambda + PutRecord.

question: Before training, an ML engineer runs the Data Wrangler data quality and insights report on a churn dataset. Which finding should make the engineer suspect target leakage?
options: About 4% of rows have a missing value in the income column
One feature alone predicts the target almost perfectly
A categorical column with 12 distinct values and no missing entries
A numeric column with a right-skewed distribution and a long tail of values
explanations: Missing values need imputation but don’t indicate leakage.
A single feature with near-perfect predictive power often encodes the outcome itself.
Moderate cardinality is normal.
Skew is a transformation issue, not leakage.
takeaway: A single “too good” feature in a quick model or report → check for target leakage.

question: A team wants to fine-tune a model in Amazon Bedrock for a multi-turn support assistant. Its examples include a system instruction, several user and assistant turns, and the ideal final reply. How should the training records be structured?
options: As single prompt and completion strings with the turns removed
As separate files for user messages and for assistant messages in S3
In the conversational format, with system, user, and assistant roles per turn
As CSV rows with one column per word in the conversation
explanations: Dropping the turns loses the conversation context the model must learn.
Splitting the turns into different files breaks the pairing between them.
Chat models are fine-tuned on role-tagged conversations that match how they are invoked.
Word-per-column CSV isn’t a supported or meaningful training format.
takeaway: Multi-turn assistants → conversational (role-based) JSONL training data.

question: A defect detection dataset contains 90% images taken in bright daylight from one factory camera. In production, cameras in dim warehouses perform poorly. Which TWO actions address this data problem? (Select TWO.)
options: Augment images with brightness and noise changes
Collect labeled images from the dim warehouse cameras
Remove the warehouse images from the validation set
Apply transfer learning from an ImageNet-pretrained model while keeping the same training images
Train for more epochs on the existing daylight images
explanations: Augmentation simulates the lighting conditions the model will see.
Real examples from the underrepresented conditions fix the gap most reliably.
Hiding the failing condition doesn’t fix it.
A better starting model doesn’t fix the missing dim-light examples in the data.
More epochs on the same skewed data increase overfitting to daylight.
takeaway: Underrepresented conditions → collect more of them and augment toward them.

topic: Pull data from an EBS volume
question: Historical training data is on an Amazon EBS volume attached to an EC2 instance. SageMaker AI training jobs need to read it. What is the simplest approach?
options: Move the volume to another Region and back to refresh it
Attach the EBS volume to the SageMaker AI training job directly
Copy the data from the instance to Amazon S3, for example with aws s3 sync
Take an EBS snapshot and point the training job at the snapshot ID
explanations: Moving the volume doesn’t make it readable by training jobs.
Training jobs can’t mount your existing EBS volumes.
Training jobs read from S3 (or EFS or FSx), so copying the data to S3 is the simplest path.
Training jobs don’t read EBS snapshots.
takeaway: Data on EBS → copy to S3 for SageMaker AI training.

question: A company is choosing between three foundation models in Amazon Bedrock for summarizing insurance claims. It has 500 example claims with reference summaries and wants an objective comparison of quality with the LEAST custom code. What should the ML engineer do?
options: Run an Amazon Bedrock evaluation job for each model on the 500 claims and compare the reports
Ask each model to rate its own summaries on a scale from 1 to 10 and keep the highest-rated model
Deploy each model to a SageMaker AI endpoint and write a scoring script that compares the outputs
Choose the model with the largest context window because it can read the longest claims
explanations: Bedrock evaluations score models on your own prompt dataset with built-in metrics and side-by-side reports.
Self-rating is biased and isn’t an objective comparison.
Self-hosting and custom scoring are far more work than a managed evaluation.
Context size alone doesn’t measure summary quality.
takeaway: Compare FMs on your own data with little code → Bedrock evaluation jobs.

question: A customer-facing chat assistant built on Amazon Bedrock must respond in under one second for short, simple questions. Quality tests show that a small model answers these questions as well as a large model. Which TWO actions will reduce response latency for users? (Select TWO.)
options: Use a cross-Region inference profile so requests can be served from other Regions
Send the requests through Bedrock batch inference
Use the smaller model that meets the quality bar
Increase the maxTokens inference parameter
Stream the response with the ConverseStream API
explanations: Cross-Region inference adds throughput and resilience; it doesn’t make each response faster.
Batch inference is asynchronous and suits offline jobs, not live chat.
Smaller models generate tokens faster and cost less per request.
A larger output limit can make responses longer and slower.
Streaming reduces the time until users see the first words.
takeaway: Latency: pick the smallest model that meets quality, and stream responses.

question: An ML engineer must adapt a 13-billion-parameter open-source model on SageMaker AI for three separate tasks. GPU memory is limited, and the team wants to store a small artifact per task instead of three full copies of the model. Which approach meets these requirements?
options: Training three smaller models from scratch, one per task, with fewer layers
Continued pre-training on a mixed dataset for all three tasks
Full fine-tuning of all model weights for each task
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning, such as LoRA adapters, for each task
explanations: Training from scratch needs far more data and compute.
Continued pre-training updates all weights on unlabeled text and doesn’t create small per-task artifacts.
Full fine-tuning needs the most GPU memory and produces a full model copy per task.
LoRA trains small adapter weights on a frozen base model, which lowers memory and keeps per-task artifacts small.
takeaway: Many tasks, limited GPU memory → PEFT/LoRA adapters on one frozen base model.

question: A company wants an assistant that answers questions about its product catalog. Prices and specifications change several times a day, and every answer must cite the source document. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
options: Put the full catalog into the system prompt of every request
RAG with a knowledge base that syncs the catalog documents often
Use continued pre-training on the catalog once per week
Fine-tune a foundation model on the catalog every night
explanations: A large, changing catalog won’t fit efficiently in every prompt and raises token costs.
RAG retrieves current documents at query time and can return citations.
Pre-training is slow and costly, and the model would still be out of date.
Nightly fine-tuning lags behind intraday changes and doesn’t provide citations.
takeaway: Frequently changing facts + citations → RAG, not fine-tuning.

question: A bank wants a model to write customer letters in a very specific structure and tone. Few-shot prompting improves results, but long prompts raise costs, and the format still varies. The bank has 8,000 approved letters with their inputs. Which approach should the ML engineer choose?
options: Fine-tune a model on the input and letter pairs
Increase the temperature so that the model follows the examples more closely
Use a larger model with the same few-shot prompt
Add the 8,000 letters to a knowledge base and retrieve examples for each request
explanations: Fine-tuning teaches a consistent format and tone and removes the need for long few-shot prompts.
Higher temperature increases variation.
A larger model raises cost and may still vary in format.
Retrieving examples still relies on prompting and adds tokens to each request.
takeaway: Consistent style or format from labeled examples → fine-tuning.

question: A credit union must explain to regulators how each input affects loan decisions, using a simple model whose coefficients can be reviewed. The data is tabular with 25 features. Which SageMaker AI built-in algorithm is the MOST appropriate starting point?
options: DeepAR
Linear Learner with binary classification
Image Classification
Object2Vec
explanations: DeepAR forecasts time series.
Logistic regression coefficients show how each feature affects the outcome.
This algorithm is for images, not tabular data.
Object2Vec learns embeddings of pairs of objects and isn’t easy to interpret.
takeaway: Interpretability requirement on tabular data → linear models (or trees with SHAP).

question: A retailer needs daily demand forecasts for 20,000 products. Many products have short sales histories, but similar products share seasonal patterns. Which SageMaker AI built-in algorithm is designed for this situation?
options: k-means
Random Cut Forest
DeepAR
Linear Learner
explanations: k-means clusters data; it doesn’t forecast.
RCF detects anomalies.
DeepAR trains one model across many related time series, which helps products with short histories.
Linear Learner is for classification and regression on independent rows, not time series.
takeaway: Many related time series → DeepAR.

question: A news company needs to classify millions of short articles into 40 topics. The team wants a SageMaker AI built-in algorithm that trains quickly on large text datasets. Which algorithm should the team use?
options: Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
Random Cut Forest
XGBoost on the raw article text
BlazingText in supervised mode
explanations: PCA reduces dimensions and doesn’t classify.
RCF is for anomaly detection.
XGBoost needs numeric features; raw text must first be converted.
BlazingText’s supervised mode is a fast text classifier that scales to large datasets.
takeaway: Fast large-scale text classification → BlazingText (supervised).

question: An e-commerce startup with no ML specialists wants personalized product recommendations that update as users click. It has interaction, item, and user data. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST ML expertise?
options: Amazon Personalize with a user personalization recipe and real-time event tracking
A Factorization Machines model on SageMaker AI with a custom retraining pipeline
A k-means model that clusters products by price
An Amazon Bedrock model that receives the full catalog in each prompt
explanations: Personalize trains and hosts recommenders from interaction data and updates with new events.
This requires ML expertise to build, tune, and operate.
Clustering by price doesn’t personalize recommendations.
Sending the catalog in every prompt is costly and isn’t a trained recommender.
takeaway: Recommendations with minimal ML work → Amazon Personalize.

question: An accounts payable team wants to extract vendor names, totals, and line items from scanned invoices with no model training. Which AWS service should the team use?
options: Amazon Comprehend custom entity recognition
Amazon Textract AnalyzeExpense
Amazon Rekognition text detection
Amazon Transcribe
explanations: This needs training data and works on text, not scanned layouts.
AnalyzeExpense extracts invoice and receipt fields and line items without training.
Rekognition finds text in images but doesn’t understand invoice fields.
Transcribe converts speech to text.
takeaway: Invoices and receipts → Textract AnalyzeExpense.

question: A hospital wants to extract medications, dosages, and medical conditions from unstructured clinical notes and link them to standard codes such as ICD-10-CM. The team has no labeled data. Which service should the team use?
options: Amazon Textract
Amazon Comprehend Medical with ontology linking
Amazon Translate
Amazon Comprehend with a custom classifier
explanations: Textract extracts text from documents but doesn’t understand medical concepts.
Comprehend Medical detects medical entities and links them to ontologies such as ICD-10-CM and RxNorm.
Translate converts between languages.
A custom classifier needs labeled data and assigns document labels, not medical entities.
takeaway: Medical entities and ontology codes → Comprehend Medical.

question: A beverage company needs to detect its own product logos in social media images. It has about 200 labeled images and no computer vision expertise. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST effort?
options: Amazon Rekognition DetectLabels with the default model
Train an object detection model from scratch on SageMaker AI
Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels
Amazon Comprehend custom entity recognition
explanations: The default labels recognize generic objects, not specific brand logos.
Training from scratch needs far more data and expertise.
Custom Labels trains a custom detector from a small labeled set without ML expertise.
Comprehend works on text, not images.
takeaway: Company-specific objects with little data or expertise → Rekognition Custom Labels.

question: A finance team stores revenue data in Amazon Redshift and wants employees to ask questions in natural language, such as “What was Q3 revenue by region?” Answers must come from the live tables. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
options: Export the tables to PDF reports weekly and add them to a vector knowledge base
Structured data retrieval from Redshift
Embed each table row and run semantic search on the vectors
Fine-tune a model on the revenue tables every month
explanations: Static exports go stale and vector search over tables is unreliable for aggregations.
Structured retrieval converts questions to SQL and runs them against the live tables.
Semantic similarity doesn’t compute sums or groupings.
A fine-tuned model can’t answer from live data and may invent numbers.
takeaway: Natural-language questions over warehouse tables → structured data retrieval (NL to SQL), not vector search.

question: A pharmaceutical research assistant must answer questions that connect entities across many documents, such as which trials studied drugs that interact with a given compound. Standard vector retrieval returns isolated chunks and misses the connections. Which RAG pattern is designed for this?
options: A higher temperature so that the model infers more connections
Fixed-size chunking with larger chunks
GraphRAG with a knowledge graph, such as Neptune Analytics
Increasing the number of retrieved chunks to 100
explanations: Higher temperature increases randomness and hallucination risk.
Larger chunks still don’t connect entities across documents.
Graph-based retrieval follows relationships between entities across documents for multi-hop questions.
More chunks add noise without modeling relationships.
takeaway: Multi-hop questions across entities → GraphRAG (knowledge graph + vectors).

question: A team must predict customer churn from 2 million rows of tabular data with 60 features. It needs good accuracy, a training time under one hour, and low cost. Which approach is the BEST fit?
options: A k-nearest neighbors model with k set to 1,000
SageMaker AI XGBoost on CPU instances
A large transformer model trained on GPU instances
Fine-tuning a foundation model on the rows as text
explanations: KNN scales poorly at prediction time and needs careful feature scaling.
XGBoost is fast, accurate on tabular data, and runs well on low-cost CPU instances.
Deep models on GPUs cost more and rarely beat tree models on tabular data.
Converting tabular rows to text for an LLM is slow, costly, and usually less accurate.
takeaway: Tabular data, tight time and cost → XGBoost (or LightGBM/CatBoost) on CPUs.

question: An XGBoost model trained with the SageMaker AI built-in algorithm has a training AUC of 0.99 and a validation AUC of 0.78. Which TWO hyperparameter changes are MOST likely to reduce overfitting? (Select TWO.)
options: Set alpha and lambda to 0
Lower subsample and colsample_bytree below 1.0
Increase num_round while keeping eta the same
Set min_child_weight to 0
Decrease max_depth
explanations: Removing regularization terms makes overfitting worse.
Sampling rows and columns for each tree adds randomness that regularizes the model.
More boosting rounds fit the training data even more closely.
Allowing splits on tiny groups makes trees more complex and increases overfitting.
Shallower trees capture fewer noise patterns.
takeaway: XGBoost overfitting → shallower trees, row/column subsampling, more regularization.

question: An ML engineer has a working PyTorch training script on a laptop and wants to train it on SageMaker AI with GPU instances. The engineer doesn’t want to build or maintain a Docker image. What should the engineer do?
options: Build a custom container with the script and push it to Amazon ECR
Run the script on a SageMaker Studio notebook instance indefinitely
Rewrite the model with the SageMaker AI XGBoost built-in algorithm
Use the SageMaker PyTorch estimator in script mode
explanations: Building and maintaining a container is what the engineer wants to avoid.
Notebook training isn’t managed, scalable, or cost-efficient.
Rewriting the model is unnecessary and may not fit the problem.
Script mode runs your script in a prebuilt PyTorch container, with no image to build.
takeaway: Existing framework script, no container work → script mode with a framework estimator.

question: A script mode training job that uses the SageMaker AI Hugging Face estimator fails with “ModuleNotFoundError: No module named ‘rapidfuzz’.” What is the simplest fix?
options: Build a new Docker image that installs every package the team might need
Switch to a larger instance type
Use Pipe input mode for the training channel
Add a requirements.txt that lists rapidfuzz to the script’s source directory
explanations: A custom image works but is much more effort than a requirements file.
Instance size doesn’t add Python packages.
Input mode controls data loading, not dependencies.
Prebuilt framework containers install packages listed in requirements.txt in the source directory.
takeaway: Extra packages in script mode → requirements.txt in source_dir.

question: An ML engineer is tuning a deep learning model with SageMaker AI automatic model tuning. Each training job takes 3 hours, and the team wants to try many configurations within a fixed budget by stopping weak configurations early and giving more resources to promising ones. Which tuning strategy should the engineer choose?
options: Grid search
Hyperband
Bayesian optimization with a maximum of two parallel jobs
Random search with no early stopping
explanations: Grid search tries every combination and wastes budget on weak areas.
Hyperband stops underperforming jobs early and reallocates resources to promising configurations.
Bayesian search is efficient but doesn’t reallocate resources across many configurations like Hyperband.
Random search runs every job to completion.
takeaway: Many expensive configurations on a budget → Hyperband.

question: A tuning job runs 100 training jobs, and many of them perform poorly after the first few epochs but continue to run until the end. How can the ML engineer reduce cost without changing the search space?
options: Set the training job early stopping type to Auto in the tuning job
Switch every training job to GPU instances
Lower the number of epochs to 1 for every job
Increase the maximum number of parallel training jobs
explanations: Automatic early stopping ends training jobs that are unlikely to beat the current best.
Faster instances don’t stop poor configurations and may cost more.
One epoch may be too few to judge good configurations.
More parallelism speeds the search but doesn’t stop poor jobs.
takeaway: Stop poor tuning trials early → early stopping type Auto.

question: A computer vision model fits in the memory of one GPU, but training on 50 million images takes 6 days on a single instance. Which approach will MOST reduce training time?
options: Model parallel training that splits the layers across GPUs
Using Pipe mode on a CPU instance
Increasing the number of epochs
Distributed data parallel training across multiple GPU instances
explanations: Model parallelism is for models that don’t fit on one GPU.
CPU instances train deep vision models far more slowly.
More epochs lengthen training.
Each GPU trains on a different shard of data, and gradients are averaged, which shortens training.
takeaway: Model fits on one GPU but data is huge → data parallelism.

question: An ML engineer is fine-tuning a 70-billion-parameter model on SageMaker AI. Training fails with CUDA out-of-memory errors on every GPU, even with a batch size of 1. Which approach should the engineer use?
options: Switch to CPU instances with more RAM
Distributed data parallel training with more GPU instances of the same type
Increase the learning rate
Sharded or model parallel training
explanations: CPU training of a 70B model would be impractically slow.
Data parallelism keeps a full model copy on each GPU, so memory errors remain.
The learning rate doesn’t affect memory use.
Sharding parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across GPUs lets a model larger than one GPU’s memory train.
takeaway: Model doesn’t fit on one GPU → model parallel or sharded (FSDP) training.

question: A team trains a model nightly for about 4 hours. It wants to cut training costs significantly and can tolerate interruptions as long as progress isn’t lost. Which TWO configurations should the team use? (Select TWO.)
options: Use a Reserved Instance for the training instances
Turn off checkpointing to reduce S3 writes
Set max_wait lower than max_run to limit waiting for Spot capacity
Save checkpoints to Amazon S3 and resume from the latest checkpoint
Enable managed spot training on the estimator
explanations: SageMaker AI training doesn’t use EC2 Reserved Instances.
Without checkpoints, interrupted jobs lose progress.
max_wait must be at least max_run; a lower value is rejected.
Checkpoints let interrupted jobs continue instead of restarting.
Managed spot training uses spare capacity at a large discount.
takeaway: Cheap, interruption-tolerant training → managed spot training + S3 checkpoints.

question: During training of a neural network, training loss keeps falling while validation loss starts rising after epoch 12. Which TWO actions will help? (Select TWO.)
options: Increase the learning rate after epoch 12
Use early stopping based on validation loss
Remove the validation set to train on more data
Train for more epochs
Add regularization, such as dropout or weight decay
explanations: A higher learning rate doesn’t address overfitting and can make training unstable.
Stopping when validation loss stops improving prevents further overfitting.
Without validation data you can’t detect overfitting.
More epochs increase overfitting.
Regularization limits how closely the model fits noise.
takeaway: Train loss ↓, validation loss ↑ → overfitting: early stopping, regularization, more data.

question: After fine-tuning a general-purpose model on legal contracts, the model performs well on contract tasks but has lost much of its ability to answer general questions that the product also needs. Which approach will BEST reduce this problem in the next training run?
options: Increase the learning rate and train for more epochs on the contracts
Remove the general questions from the evaluation set
Fine-tune again on contracts with a larger batch size
Mix general examples into the training data and use PEFT
explanations: More aggressive training on one domain increases forgetting.
Hiding the problem doesn’t fix it.
Batch size alone doesn’t protect general capabilities.
Rehearsal data and adapters that keep base weights frozen both reduce catastrophic forgetting.
takeaway: Catastrophic forgetting → mix in general data, use PEFT, lower learning rate.

question: A support team classifies 1 million tickets a day with a large foundation model, and costs are high. Analysis shows that 85% of tickets are simple and a small fine-tuned model handles them accurately when it is confident. Which design will reduce cost while keeping accuracy?
options: Average the predictions of the small and large models for every ticket
Send tickets to the small model first; escalate low-confidence ones
Replace the large model with the small model for every ticket
Use the large model with batch inference for urgent tickets
explanations: Calling both models for every ticket increases cost.
A cascade uses the cheap model for most tickets and reserves the large model for hard cases.
The small model is less accurate on the hard 15% of tickets.
Batch inference is asynchronous and doesn’t suit urgent tickets.
takeaway: Combine models to cut cost → cascade (cheap model first, escalate uncertain cases).

question: The training loss of a model jumps up and down sharply between steps and doesn’t trend downward. The data pipeline and labels are correct. Which change should the ML engineer try FIRST?
options: Increase the number of epochs
Remove the validation set
Decrease the learning rate
Increase the learning rate
explanations: More epochs repeat the unstable updates.
The validation set doesn’t affect training updates.
Large updates overshoot the minimum; smaller steps let the loss decrease steadily.
A higher learning rate makes the oscillation worse.
takeaway: Oscillating or diverging loss → lower the learning rate.

question: A model was trained for 50 epochs. Validation loss reached its lowest value at epoch 9 and increased afterward. What should the ML engineer do for the next training run?
options: Keep 50 epochs and increase the batch size
Train for 100 epochs to let the model recover
Use about 9–10 epochs or enable early stopping on validation loss
Reduce the training data to make each epoch faster
explanations: This doesn’t address training past the best point.
Validation loss is already increasing; more epochs overfit further.
Stopping near the best validation epoch avoids overfitting and saves time.
Less data usually hurts generalization.
takeaway: Stop around the best validation epoch (or use early stopping).

question: An application asks a Bedrock model to extract order details and return JSON. About 10% of responses include extra text or use different field names, which breaks the parser. Which approach will improve consistency with the LEAST effort?
options: Raise the temperature so that the model explores formats
Give the JSON schema in the prompt plus a few complete examples
Fine-tune the model on 10,000 labeled orders
Switch to a model with a larger context window and a higher output limit
explanations: Higher temperature increases variation.
Clear format instructions with few-shot examples make the output format consistent.
Fine-tuning works but is far more effort than improving the prompt.
Context size doesn’t control output format.
takeaway: Format problems → schema instructions + few-shot examples before fine-tuning.

question: A RAG application over engineering documents fails to retrieve passages when users search for part numbers such as “XR-2044-B,” although semantic questions work well. Which change will MOST improve retrieval for these queries?
options: Use hybrid search so that keyword matching complements semantic search
Lower the temperature of the generation model
Increase the chunk size to 2,000 tokens
Use a larger generation model
explanations: Keyword (lexical) matching finds exact identifiers that embeddings represent poorly.
Temperature affects generation, not retrieval.
Larger chunks dilute exact matches.
Generation can’t fix passages that weren’t retrieved.
takeaway: Exact codes or IDs missed by vectors → hybrid search.

question: A knowledge base returns the correct passage within its top 20 results, but often not in the top 3 that are sent to the model. Which change will MOST improve answer quality?
options: Use fixed-size chunking with no overlap so that each passage is distinct
Retrieve more, then rerank
Switch to a smaller embedding model
Reduce the number of retrieved results to 1
explanations: Chunking changes don’t fix the ranking order.
Rerankers rescore candidate passages for relevance to the query, which moves the best passages to the top.
A smaller embedding model usually lowers retrieval quality.
This makes it less likely that the correct passage is included.
takeaway: Right passage retrieved but ranked low → reranking.

question: A team runs hundreds of training experiments with different features and hyperparameters. It needs to log parameters, metrics, and artifacts for every run, compare runs in a UI, and register the best model. Which SageMaker AI capability should the team use?
options: Amazon S3 Inventory
AWS CloudTrail
Managed MLflow on SageMaker AI
Amazon CloudWatch Logs
explanations: Inventory lists objects; it doesn’t track experiments.
CloudTrail records API calls, not experiment metrics.
MLflow tracks runs, compares them, and can register models to SageMaker Model Registry.
Logs aren’t organized for comparing parameters and metrics across runs.
takeaway: Reproducible experiment tracking → MLflow on SageMaker AI.

question: A team is testing prompt variations for a Bedrock application. Engineers overwrite each other’s prompts in a shared document, and the team can’t tell which prompt version produced which evaluation result. Which solution will make prompt experiments reproducible?
options: Use Bedrock Prompt Management with a version per tested prompt
Ask each engineer to keep a personal, dated copy of the prompts they test
Store prompts as comments in the application code
Set the model’s temperature to 0 for all tests
explanations: Prompt Management stores prompts with variables and variants, and versions make each test reproducible.
Personal copies make reproducibility worse.
Comments don’t version prompts or link them to evaluations.
Temperature helps consistency but doesn’t track prompt versions.
takeaway: Version and reuse prompts → Bedrock Prompt Management.

question: An ML engineer is building a pipeline that detects data drift for a tabular model in production. What should the engineer create FIRST so that production data has a reference for comparison?
options: A larger held-out test set that is sampled from the original training data
A confusion matrix from the latest production week
A CloudWatch alarm on endpoint latency
A training data baseline
explanations: A test set alone isn’t a statistical reference for monitoring.
This needs ground truth and doesn’t describe expected input distributions.
Latency alarms don’t describe the input data distribution.
Drift checks compare production feature distributions with a baseline from training data.
takeaway: Drift detection starts with a baseline of training data statistics.

question: A team has trained a new version of a fraud model and wants to compare its latency and predictions with the current model on real production traffic, without any customer receiving the new model’s predictions. Which approach should the team use?
options: A canary deployment that shifts 10% of traffic
Batch transform on last month’s data
A SageMaker AI shadow test with the new model as a shadow variant
A/B testing with 50% of traffic sent to the new model
explanations: Canary traffic is served by the new model.
Historical batch data isn’t live production traffic.
Shadow variants receive a copy of production requests, but their responses aren’t returned to callers.
In an A/B test, customers receive responses from the new model.
takeaway: Compare on live traffic with no customer impact → shadow testing.

question: A lender must tell each rejected applicant which factors most influenced their individual decision. Which technique provides these per-prediction explanations?
options: A confusion matrix for the model
Global feature importance from the training run
SHAP values for each prediction
The ROC curve for the model
explanations: A confusion matrix summarizes overall errors, not individual decisions.
Global importance doesn’t explain a single applicant’s result.
SHAP attributes each prediction to the features that pushed it up or down.
ROC curves describe threshold trade-offs across all predictions.
takeaway: Per-prediction explanations → SHAP (local feature attributions).

question: A data science team wants to show business stakeholders how the predicted probability of churn changes, on average, as monthly price increases across all customers. Which explanation technique is designed for this?
options: An AUC comparison between two models
A partial dependence plot (PDP) for monthly price
SHAP values for a single customer
A confusion matrix at several thresholds
explanations: AUC compares model ranking quality.
A PDP shows the average change in predictions as one feature varies.
Single-customer SHAP values explain one prediction, not the average effect.
Confusion matrices don’t show how a feature affects predictions.
takeaway: Average effect of one feature → partial dependence plot.

question: While training a recurrent neural network, the loss suddenly becomes NaN after a few hundred steps. Gradient norms logged by the training script grow very large just before the failure. Which TWO actions should the ML engineer take? (Select TWO.)
options: Remove the activation functions
Apply gradient clipping
Increase the number of epochs
Lower the learning rate
Increase the batch size tenfold and the learning rate tenfold
explanations: Removing non-linearities breaks the model’s ability to learn.
Clipping caps gradient norms and prevents exploding updates.
Training longer doesn’t fix diverging gradients.
Smaller steps reduce the chance of numerical overflow.
A much larger learning rate makes divergence more likely.
takeaway: NaN loss with huge gradients → gradient clipping and a lower learning rate.

question: A model screens medical images for a serious disease. Missing a positive case is far more costly than sending a healthy patient for a follow-up test. Which metric should the team prioritize?
options: Specificity
Recall
Accuracy
Precision
explanations: Specificity measures how well negatives are identified.
Recall measures the share of actual positives the model finds, so it penalizes missed cases.
Accuracy can look high even when rare positives are missed.
Precision focuses on avoiding false positives.
takeaway: Costly false negatives → maximize recall.

question: An email security model moves suspected phishing emails to quarantine. Users complain that legitimate business emails are often quarantined. Which metric should the team improve?
options: Precision
Perplexity
Mean absolute error
Recall
explanations: Precision measures how many quarantined emails are really phishing, so it penalizes false positives.
Perplexity evaluates language models.
MAE is a regression metric.
Recall focuses on catching every phishing email.
takeaway: Costly false positives → improve precision.

question: A delivery time model is evaluated on data that includes occasional extreme delays caused by storms. The business wants a metric that reflects typical errors and isn’t dominated by these rare extremes. Which metric should the team use?
options: R-squared on the training set
F1 score
Root mean squared error (RMSE)
Mean absolute error (MAE)
explanations: Training-set R² doesn’t measure generalization and doesn’t address outliers.
F1 is a classification metric.
Squaring errors makes RMSE sensitive to large outliers.
MAE weights all errors linearly, so rare extremes have less influence.
takeaway: Outlier-robust regression error → MAE; penalize large errors → RMSE.

question: Two binary classifiers will be used with different decision thresholds by different teams. The ML engineer needs a single metric that compares how well each model ranks positives above negatives across all thresholds. Which metric should the engineer use?
options: Mean squared error of the labels
Precision at a threshold of 0.9
Accuracy at a threshold of 0.5
Area under the ROC curve (AUC)
explanations: MSE isn’t the standard ranking metric for classifiers.
Precision also depends on one threshold.
Accuracy depends on one threshold.
AUC summarizes performance across all thresholds.
takeaway: Compare classifiers across thresholds → AUC.

question: A company wants subject-matter experts from its own legal team to rate and compare responses from two Bedrock models for tone and legal soundness, which automated metrics can’t judge reliably. Which solution should the ML engineer use?
options: A CloudWatch dashboard of token counts
An Amazon Rekognition content moderation job
An automatic model evaluation job with the built-in toxicity metric
A human-based evaluation job
explanations: Token counts don’t measure response quality.
Rekognition moderates images and videos.
Toxicity scores don’t capture legal soundness or tone preferences.
Human-based evaluation jobs let your own experts rate and compare model responses.
takeaway: Subjective expert judgment → Bedrock human-based evaluation with your own team.

question: A team evaluates a model on two tasks: summarizing support tickets and translating them into Spanish. It has reference outputs for both tasks. Which TWO metrics are commonly used for these tasks? (Select TWO.)
options: ROUGE for the summaries
Mean absolute error for both tasks
Word error rate for the summaries
BLEU for the translations
AUC for the translations
explanations: ROUGE measures n-gram overlap with reference summaries, with an emphasis on recall.
MAE is a regression metric.
WER is used for speech recognition transcripts.
BLEU measures n-gram precision against reference translations.
AUC is a classification metric.
takeaway: Summaries → ROUGE; translations → BLEU.

question: A summarization model often produces correct summaries that use different words from the reference summaries, so ROUGE scores are low even when human reviewers rate the summaries highly. Which metric better reflects meaning?
options: Perplexity
Word error rate
BLEU
BERTScore
explanations: Perplexity measures how well a model predicts text, not similarity to a reference.
WER counts word-level edits and penalizes paraphrases.
BLEU is also based on exact n-gram overlap.
BERTScore compares contextual embeddings, so paraphrases with the same meaning score well.
takeaway: Paraphrase-tolerant similarity → BERTScore (embedding-based).

question: A team needs to evaluate 20,000 chatbot responses for correctness, completeness, and helpfulness every week. Human review of all responses is too slow and expensive. Which approach will meet these requirements with the LEAST effort?
options: A Bedrock evaluation job that uses a judge model
Ask the chatbot to grade its own responses inline
Compute BLEU scores for every response
Count the tokens in each response
explanations: An evaluator LLM scores each response on metrics such as correctness, completeness, and helpfulness and explains the score.
Self-grading inside the same call is biased and unstructured.
BLEU needs reference texts and doesn’t judge helpfulness.
Length isn’t a quality measure.
takeaway: Scalable qualitative scoring → LLM-as-a-judge evaluations.

question: Before launch, a company must check whether its Bedrock-based assistant produces stereotypes about demographic groups in its responses. Which evaluation approach should the team use?
options: Compare the training and validation loss curves of the underlying model
Measure ROUGE against reference answers
Run a judge-model evaluation that uses the Stereotyping metric
Run a Glue Data Quality job on the prompts
explanations: Loss curves don’t reveal stereotyping in outputs.
Overlap metrics don’t detect stereotypes.
Bedrock’s Stereotyping metric flags responses that contain stereotypes about groups.
Data quality rules check data structure, not model behavior.
takeaway: Stereotypes in LLM outputs → evaluate with the Stereotyping (responsible AI) metric.

question: A team wants to know whether poor answers from its RAG application come from retrieval or from generation. It has questions with ground-truth passages. Which evaluation should the team run first to isolate retrieval quality?
options: A retrieve-only RAG evaluation job
A latency test of the knowledge base API
A model evaluation job on the generation model without the knowledge base
A human evaluation of the final answers’ tone
explanations: Retrieve-only evaluation scores the retrieved passages, which isolates retrieval problems.
Latency doesn’t measure retrieval accuracy.
This tests the model alone and ignores retrieval.
Tone doesn’t show whether the right passages were retrieved.
takeaway: Isolate retrieval quality → retrieve-only RAG evaluation (context relevance/coverage).

question: An assistant must answer questions about 200-page technical specifications in a single request, without a retrieval system. Which model property matters MOST when choosing the foundation model?
options: The model’s image generation quality and resolution
The number of languages the model was trained on
The maximum number of output tokens the model can generate
A context window large enough to hold the whole document at once
explanations: Image generation is unrelated to reading long text.
Language coverage matters only if the documents use several languages.
Output length doesn’t determine how much input fits.
The full document must fit in the model’s context window for single-request answers.
takeaway: Whole documents in one request → context window size (or use RAG instead).

question: An insurance app must accept a photo of vehicle damage plus a short text description and return a written assessment. Which kind of foundation model is required?
options: A model that accepts text input with a large context window
A multimodal model that accepts image and text input
An embedding model for images and text
An image generation model that creates damage photos
explanations: A text-only model can’t read the photo.
The model must understand both the photo and the text to write the assessment.
Embedding models produce vectors, not written assessments.
The task is to analyze an image, not to create one.
takeaway: Image + text in, text out → multimodal (vision-language) model.

question: A marketing team wants to group customers into segments based on purchase behavior. It has no labels for the segments. Which SageMaker AI built-in algorithm fits?
options: Object Detection on purchase receipts
k-means
Linear Learner with a binary classifier
DeepAR for many related time series
explanations: Object detection finds objects in images.
k-means is unsupervised clustering that groups similar customers.
Linear Learner is supervised and needs labels.
DeepAR forecasts time series.
takeaway: Unlabeled grouping → k-means (clustering).

question: An ad platform predicts click-through rates from very sparse, high-dimensional data: user IDs, ad IDs, and their pairwise interactions. Which SageMaker AI built-in algorithm is designed for this?
options: BlazingText in Word2Vec mode
Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
Random Cut Forest with default settings
Factorization Machines
explanations: BlazingText works on text.
PCA reduces dimensions but doesn’t predict clicks.
RCF finds anomalies, not click probabilities.
Factorization Machines model pairwise interactions in sparse data, common for recommendations and CTR.
takeaway: Sparse interactions (users × items, CTR) → Factorization Machines.

question: A bank wants to flag logins where a user signs in from an IP address that is unusual for that user. It has historical pairs of user IDs and IP addresses. Which SageMaker AI built-in algorithm is built for this?
options: IP Insights
Linear Learner trained on IP address strings
Image Classification on screenshots of the logins
Seq2Seq trained on the login history
explanations: IP Insights learns usage patterns of entity–IP address pairs and scores how unusual a new pair is.
IP strings aren’t meaningful numeric features for a linear model.
The data isn’t images.
Seq2Seq maps input sequences to output sequences, such as translation.
takeaway: Entity–IP pair anomalies → IP Insights.

question: A retailer has three computer vision needs: (1) say whether a shelf photo contains any empty spaces, (2) draw boxes around each product, and (3) label every pixel that belongs to the floor. Which SageMaker AI built-in algorithms match needs 2 and 3? (Select TWO.)
options: Image Classification in multi-label mode for drawing product boxes
Object Detection for labeling every pixel that belongs to the floor
k-means clustering for labeling floor pixels
Semantic Segmentation for labeling floor pixels
Object Detection for drawing boxes around products
explanations: Image Classification assigns labels to the whole image; it doesn’t draw boxes.
Object Detection draws boxes; per-pixel labels need Semantic Segmentation.
k-means groups unlabeled data; it isn’t a supervised segmentation algorithm.
Semantic segmentation classifies every pixel.
Object detection returns bounding boxes and labels for objects.
takeaway: Whole image → classification; boxes → object detection; pixels → semantic segmentation.

question: A company needs a text and voice chatbot that collects a booking date and destination, then calls a booking API. The team wants a managed service designed around intents and slots. Which service should it use?
options: Amazon Translate
Amazon Textract
Amazon Lex
Amazon Polly
explanations: Translate converts text between languages.
Textract extracts text from documents.
Lex builds bots with intents and slots and can call Lambda functions.
Polly converts text to speech.
takeaway: Intent/slot chatbots → Amazon Lex.

question: Amazon Transcribe keeps misspelling the company’s product names, such as “Zyntra” and “Qubix,” in call transcripts. Which feature fixes this with the LEAST effort?
options: Content redaction of the product names
A custom vocabulary
Speaker diarization for each call
Training a new speech model on SageMaker AI
explanations: Redaction removes text; it doesn’t correct it.
A custom vocabulary teaches Transcribe how to recognize specific terms.
Diarization identifies speakers, not vocabulary.
Training a model from scratch is far more effort.
takeaway: Domain terms in speech → Transcribe custom vocabulary (custom language model for broader domain text).

question: Amazon Translate translates the brand name “Swift Ledger” into a different phrase in each language, but marketing wants it left unchanged. What should the ML engineer use?
options: Batch translation instead of real-time translation
A larger instance type for the translation endpoint
Custom terminology
Automatic language detection for every request
explanations: The processing mode doesn’t change how terms are translated.
Translate is serverless; there is no instance to size.
Custom terminology tells Translate exactly how to translate (or keep) specific terms.
Detecting the source language doesn’t control terms.
takeaway: Brand or domain terms in translation → custom terminology.

question: In a RAG chat assistant, users ask follow-up questions such as “What about for contractors?” Retrieval for these follow-ups returns irrelevant passages because the query lacks context. Which TWO changes help? (Select TWO.)
options: Rewrite each follow-up into a standalone query using the chat history before retrieval
Increase the number of retrieved results from 5 to 50 for every follow-up question
Lower the temperature of the generation model
Re-embed the documents with a larger embedding model
Use the knowledge base’s session-aware RetrieveAndGenerate with a session ID
explanations: Query rewriting adds the missing context (for example the policy being discussed).
More results for a context-free query mostly add more irrelevant passages.
Temperature affects generation, not retrieval.
The problem is the query, which lacks context, not the document embeddings.
Passing the session lets the service use prior turns when forming the query.
takeaway: Context-free follow-ups → query rewriting / session-aware retrieval.

question: An analyst assistant must answer questions such as “Compare last quarter’s churn with the targets in our strategy document and suggest actions.” This needs a SQL query, a document lookup, and reasoning across both results. Which approach fits BEST?
options: A larger context window with every table pasted into the prompt
An agent that calls SQL and retrieval tools, then reasons
Fine-tuning a model on last quarter’s numbers
A single vector search over all documents
explanations: Pasting whole tables is costly and error-prone.
Agentic RAG plans multiple tool calls and combines their results.
Fine-tuning bakes in stale numbers and can’t query live data.
One vector search can’t run SQL or combine results.
takeaway: Multi-step questions across tools → agentic RAG.

question: An ML engineer is comparing 12 feature sets for a model trained on 2 billion rows. Each full training run takes 9 hours. How can the engineer choose a feature set faster at low cost?
options: Choose the feature set with the most features
Run all 12 full trainings in sequence on the largest instance
Compare on a representative sample; train the winner fully
Skip validation and deploy all 12 models to compare in production
explanations: More features don’t guarantee better performance.
Full runs for every option are slow and expensive.
Sampling speeds up iteration; the final model still uses all the data.
Deploying untested models risks production quality.
takeaway: Fast iteration → experiment on samples, then train on full data.

question: A high-volume classification feature uses a large foundation model. Quality is good, but per-request cost and latency are too high. The team has many logged prompts but no labels. Which approach reduces cost and latency while keeping quality?
options: Add more examples to every prompt
Increase maxTokens so responses are more complete
Distill the large model into a smaller model
Buy Provisioned Throughput for the large model
explanations: Longer prompts raise cost and latency.
Longer outputs increase cost and latency.
Distillation trains a smaller, faster student to match the teacher on your prompts.
Provisioned capacity guarantees throughput but doesn’t make the model smaller or faster per token.
takeaway: Same quality, smaller and cheaper → distillation.

question: A team notices that time-to-first-token for its Bedrock application grew after it added 20 long examples to every prompt. Which TWO actions will reduce latency? (Select TWO.)
options: Cache the stable prompt prefix with prompt caching
Switch to a model with a larger context window
Remove examples that don’t improve quality
Switch to batch inference for live users
Send each request twice and keep the faster one
explanations: Cached prefixes are processed faster on later calls.
The prompt already fits; a larger window doesn’t reduce the time to process it.
Fewer input tokens shorten the time to process the prompt.
Batch inference is asynchronous.
Duplicate requests double cost and load.
takeaway: Long prompts slow time-to-first-token → trim and cache.

question: A support team wants to route incoming emails into 15 categories. It has 20,000 labeled emails and no ML engineers. Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST effort?
options: Train an Amazon Comprehend custom classifier
Use Amazon Comprehend keyphrase extraction to guess categories
Write regex rules for each category
Train a custom transformer model in a SageMaker AI notebook
explanations: Comprehend custom classification trains from labeled text with no ML code.
Key phrases don’t map reliably to 15 business categories.
Hand-written rules are brittle and need constant maintenance.
Custom deep learning needs ML engineering effort.
takeaway: Labeled text into custom categories with little effort → Comprehend custom classification.

question: An ML engineer uploads training data in CSV format for the SageMaker AI built-in XGBoost algorithm. How must the CSV be structured?
options: With a header row and the label in the last column of each row
Without a header row, with the label in the first column
With the label stored in a separate file per row
With one JSON object per line and a label field
explanations: The built-in algorithm expects no header and the label first.
Built-in algorithms that read CSV expect the target in the first column and no header.
Labels are part of each CSV row.
That describes JSON Lines, not CSV.
takeaway: Built-in algorithms with CSV: no header, label first.

question: An ML engineer trains Linear Learner to predict one of 6 product categories. Which hyperparameter setting is required?
options: predictor_type multiclass_classifier, num_classes 6
predictor_type set to binary_classifier with 6 outputs
predictor_type set to regressor with rounded outputs
feature_dim set to 6 to match the six categories
explanations: Multiclass classification needs the multiclass predictor type and the number of classes.
Binary classification handles two classes.
Regression predicts a number.
feature_dim is the number of input features, not classes.
takeaway: Linear Learner tasks are set by predictor_type (binary, multiclass, regressor).

question: In a SageMaker AI script mode training job, how does the training script find the training data and the hyperparameters passed to the estimator?
options: SM_CHANNEL_* environment variables and script arguments
From hard-coded S3 paths that must be edited before each run
By downloading them from the notebook that started the job
From a DynamoDB table that SageMaker creates for each job
explanations: SageMaker sets environment variables such as SM_CHANNEL_TRAIN and passes hyperparameters as script arguments.
Hard-coded paths defeat the purpose of input channels.
The job runs on separate instances without access to the notebook.
SageMaker doesn’t create DynamoDB tables for jobs.
takeaway: Script mode: data paths via SM_CHANNEL_* / SM_MODEL_DIR; hyperparameters as CLI args.

question: An ML engineer ran a tuning job last week. The data hasn’t changed, and the engineer wants a new tuning job to start from what the previous job learned instead of searching from scratch. Which feature should the engineer use?
options: Pipeline step caching
Managed warm pools with a long keep-alive period
A larger maximum number of training jobs
Warm start with IDENTICAL_DATA_AND_ALGORITHM as the type
explanations: Caching skips identical pipeline steps; it doesn’t guide a new search.
Warm pools reuse provisioned instances, not tuning knowledge.
More jobs search longer but still start from scratch.
Warm start uses earlier tuning jobs’ results as prior knowledge for the new search.
takeaway: Continue a past search → AMT warm start (identical data/algorithm or transfer learning).

question: An ML engineer tunes a learning rate between 0.00001 and 0.1. Which scaling type should the hyperparameter range use?
options: Logarithmic scaling
Reverse logarithmic scaling
Linear scaling
Integer scaling
explanations: Log scaling samples evenly across orders of magnitude.
Reverse logarithmic suits values close to 1, such as momentum.
Linear scaling would spend most trials on large values.
A learning rate is a continuous value.
takeaway: Ranges spanning orders of magnitude → logarithmic scaling.

question: An ML engineer tunes a custom PyTorch script with SageMaker AI automatic model tuning. The tuning job fails because it can’t find the objective metric. The script prints lines such as “val_f1=0.842” each epoch. What must the engineer add?
options: An environment variable named OBJECTIVE=f1
A metric definition regex that captures val_f1
A CloudWatch alarm on the val_f1 value
A larger instance so the metric is computed faster
explanations: There’s no such convention.
Custom scripts need metric definitions so SageMaker can parse the objective from the logs.
Alarms don’t feed metrics to the tuner.
Speed doesn’t make the metric visible to the tuner.
takeaway: Custom training scripts → metric_definitions (regex on logs) for tuning and metrics.

question: A PyTorch training job on ml.p4d instances shows GPUs at 35% utilization while the data loader is busy. Which TWO changes will MOST likely shorten training? (Select TWO.)
options: Add data loader workers and use a faster input path, such as FSx for Lustre
Add more GPU instances while keeping the same data pipeline
Switch to larger ml.p5 instances with faster GPUs while keeping the same data loader settings
Use mixed precision (bf16) training
Write a checkpoint to Amazon S3 after every training step
explanations: Feeding data faster removes the bottleneck that leaves GPUs idle.
More GPUs would wait on the same slow pipeline.
Faster GPUs would wait on the same slow data pipeline.
Lower-precision math speeds up GPU computation and reduces memory use.
Frequent checkpoints add I/O and slow training further.
takeaway: Low GPU utilization → fix the input pipeline first; then mixed precision.

question: A model has high error on both the training data and the validation data, and the two errors are similar. Which TWO actions are MOST likely to help? (Select TWO.)
options: Add dropout and stronger weight decay
Add more informative features
Increase L2 regularization strength
Use a more expressive model or add model capacity
Remove half of the features at random
explanations: Regularization fights overfitting; this model is underfitting.
Better features give the model signal to learn from.
Stronger regularization makes underfitting worse.
More capacity lets the model capture patterns it currently misses.
Removing features reduces the available signal.
takeaway: Underfitting (high train and validation error) → more capacity, better features, less regularization.

question: A linear model uses 5,000 features, and stakeholders want a simpler model that keeps only the most useful ones. Which regularization approach drives many feature weights to exactly zero?
options: L2 (ridge) regularization
Early stopping
L1 (lasso) regularization
Dropout
explanations: L2 shrinks weights toward zero but rarely makes them exactly zero.
Early stopping limits training time, not the number of nonzero weights.
L1 regularization produces sparse models by setting many weights to zero.
Dropout regularizes neural networks during training, not linear weight sparsity.
takeaway: Sparse, simpler linear models → L1 regularization.

question: Three different models each reach about 0.88 AUC on a validation set, and their errors are only partly correlated. How can the ML engineer combine them to improve accuracy?
options: Keep the model with the shortest training time
Train each model again on a different half of the data
Stack them: train a meta-model on their predictions
Average their hyperparameters into one new model
explanations: This discards useful information from the others.
Less data usually hurts each model.
Stacking learns how to combine models whose errors differ.
Hyperparameters can’t be averaged into a meaningful model.
takeaway: Diverse models with uncorrelated errors → ensemble (stacking, averaging, voting).

question: An ML engineer increases the batch size from 32 to 1,024 to speed up training on GPUs. Training is faster per epoch, but validation accuracy drops. What is a common adjustment?
options: Retune the learning rate (often higher, with warm-up)
Switch the optimizer to plain random search
Decrease the number of GPUs to slow each step down
Remove the validation set
explanations: Large batches change gradient noise and usually need a retuned learning rate schedule.
Random search is a tuning strategy, not an optimizer.
Fewer GPUs doesn’t address the accuracy drop.
Removing validation hides the problem.
takeaway: Bigger batches → retune learning rate (with warm-up).

question: A model makes arithmetic and multi-step logic mistakes when calculating refund amounts. Which prompt technique MOST improves accuracy on these questions?
options: Remove the policy text and rely on the model’s memory
Ask it to reason step by step, then answer
Ask for the shortest possible answer with no explanation
Raise the temperature to 1.0 for more creative answers
explanations: Without the policy, answers become guesses.
Chain-of-thought prompting improves multi-step reasoning.
Forcing brevity removes the reasoning that helps accuracy.
Creativity increases variation, not correctness.
takeaway: Multi-step reasoning → chain-of-thought prompting (plus clear rules).

question: An assistant must always answer as a polite banking agent, refuse topics outside banking, and use British English. Where should these standing instructions go?
options: In the system prompt
In each user message, typed by the customer
In the stop sequences parameter
In the model’s training data by fine-tuning every week
explanations: The system prompt sets persistent role, scope, and style instructions for the conversation.
Customers shouldn’t have to repeat instructions.
Stop sequences end generation; they don’t carry instructions.
Fine-tuning is unnecessary for simple standing instructions.
takeaway: Persistent role, scope, and style → system prompt (plus guardrails for enforcement).

question: A team must classify support tickets into 8 categories. Few-shot prompting with 3 examples per category reaches 91% accuracy, which meets the target, but the team wants better consistency. Which TWO actions are reasonable next steps before fine-tuning? (Select TWO.)
options: Fine-tune a model from scratch on 50 tickets
Increase temperature to 0.9 so the model considers more possible labels for each ticket
Use temperature 0 and a fixed label format
Remove the category definitions from the prompt
Choose clearer, more representative examples for each category
explanations: Training from scratch on 50 examples won’t work.
Higher temperature makes outputs less consistent, the opposite of the goal.
Deterministic settings and a strict format reduce variation.
Definitions guide the model’s choices.
Better examples often improve few-shot accuracy and consistency.
takeaway: Before fine-tuning: better examples, clear format, low temperature.

question: A biotech RAG application retrieves poorly because its embedding model doesn’t capture the similarity between internal compound names and their descriptions. The team has thousands of query–passage pairs. Which approach will MOST improve retrieval?
options: Fine-tune the embedding model on those pairs
Use a larger generation model
Increase the number of retrieved chunks to 200
Lower the chunk overlap to 0%
explanations: Fine-tuning embeddings on in-domain pairs teaches the model domain-specific similarity.
Generation can’t fix poor retrieval.
More chunks add noise and cost.
Overlap doesn’t teach domain vocabulary.
takeaway: Domain-specific similarity → fine-tune the embedding model (hybrid search for exact terms).

question: An ML engineer wants to choose the best chunk size and number of retrieved results for a knowledge base. What is the MOST reliable approach?
options: Ask users to report bad answers for a month
Pick the largest chunk size so that answers have more context
Evaluate each configuration on a labeled question set
Use the same settings as a public benchmark
explanations: User reports are slow and incomplete.
Larger chunks can dilute relevance; the choice should be measured.
Measured context relevance and coverage show which settings work for your data.
Benchmarks don’t reflect your documents and questions.
takeaway: Tune retrieval settings with RAG evaluations on a labeled question set.

question: Two runs of the same training code produce noticeably different models, and the team can’t explain why. Which TWO practices make runs reproducible? (Select TWO.)
options: Shuffle the data differently each time without a seed
Use a different instance type for every run
Record the dataset version and hyperparameters of each run, for example in MLflow
Fix random seeds and pin library and container versions
Train on a larger instance type so each run finishes sooner
explanations: Unseeded shuffles cause the variation.
Changing hardware adds variation.
Tracking inputs makes runs repeatable and comparable.
Seeds and pinned versions remove hidden sources of variation.
Speed doesn’t fix randomness or untracked inputs.
takeaway: Reproducibility = seeds + pinned environments + tracked data and parameters.

question: Before investing in a complex model for predicting late deliveries, an ML engineer wants a reference point to judge whether ML adds value. What should the engineer build first?
options: A dashboard of the delivery trucks’ locations
A large ensemble of deep neural networks to compare
A simple rule or logistic regression baseline
A larger training dataset
explanations: A dashboard isn’t a predictive baseline.
Complex models are the thing being judged, not the reference.
A simple baseline shows how much a complex model actually improves.
More data doesn’t provide a comparison point.
takeaway: Always compare against a simple baseline.

question: Input distributions for a fraud model look stable, but fraud losses are rising. Investigators confirm labels 2 weeks after each transaction. What kind of drift is MOST likely, and how should it be detected?
options: No drift; increase the decision threshold
Bias drift; compare approval rates between age groups
Concept drift; track quality on labeled outcomes
Data drift; compare input statistics with the training baseline
explanations: Rising losses indicate a real change.
Group fairness isn’t the reported problem.
When the input-to-label relationship changes, quality metrics on ground truth reveal it.
Inputs are stable, so data drift checks won’t show it.
takeaway: Stable inputs + falling outcomes → concept drift; detect with model quality on ground truth.

question: A shadow variant ran for a week. Which result would justify promoting it to production?
options: It returned responses to more customers than the production variant
It produced different predictions for every request
Healthy operations and better accuracy
Its endpoint used a larger instance type
explanations: Shadow variants don’t return responses to customers.
Disagreement alone doesn’t mean it’s better.
Promotion needs operational safety and evidence of better quality.
Instance size alone isn’t a reason to promote.
takeaway: Promote a shadow variant on operational health + better measured quality.

question: A regulator asks which features drive a credit model’s decisions across all applicants. Which explanation should the ML engineer provide?
options: The model’s training and validation loss curves
The confusion matrix at a decision threshold of 0.5
Mean absolute SHAP values across many predictions
SHAP values for one approved applicant
explanations: Loss curves describe training, not feature influence.
Confusion matrices describe errors, not drivers.
Averaging SHAP magnitudes across predictions gives global feature importance.
One applicant’s explanation doesn’t describe the model overall.
takeaway: Global drivers → aggregated SHAP (mean |SHAP|) or global importance; individual → local SHAP.
