question: A deep network’s early layers barely change during training, and the loss decreases very slowly. Gradient norms for early layers are close to zero. Which TWO changes help? (Select TWO.)
options: Increase the depth of the network
Lower the learning rate by 1,000 times
Switch hidden-layer activations from ReLU to sigmoid to keep outputs between 0 and 1
Add batch normalization or residual connections
Use ReLU-family activations instead of sigmoid in hidden layers
explanations: More layers make vanishing gradients worse.
Smaller steps slow training even more.
Sigmoid saturates and makes vanishing gradients worse.
Normalization and skip connections help gradients flow to early layers.
Sigmoid saturates and shrinks gradients; ReLU-style activations keep them larger.
takeaway: Vanishing gradients → ReLU-type activations, normalization, residual connections, good initialization.

question: Training loss drops quickly for a few epochs and then stays flat at a value that is still too high, while validation loss follows the same pattern. Which change is MOST likely to help?
options: Train with a constant, higher learning rate
A learning rate schedule (decay or warm restarts)
Reduce the training data by half
Remove the validation set to free up more training data
explanations: A higher constant rate tends to bounce around the plateau.
Changing the learning rate over time helps the optimizer settle into better minima.
Less data rarely helps optimization.
This hides information without helping.
takeaway: Plateau at a high loss → learning rate schedule (and check model capacity).

question: A classifier’s confusion matrix shows 80 true positives, 20 false positives, 40 false negatives, and 860 true negatives. What is its precision?
explanations: This is accuracy: (80 + 860) ÷ 1,000.
This is recall: 80 ÷ (80 + 40).
Precision = TP ÷ (TP + FP) = 80 ÷ 100.
takeaway: Precision = TP/(TP+FP); recall = TP/(TP+FN).

question: Why is the F1 score useful for an imbalanced classification problem?
options: It balances precision and recall in one number
It is based on true negatives, which dominate imbalanced data
It equals accuracy on any dataset
It measures how fast the model makes predictions
explanations: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, so both must be good.
F1 ignores true negatives.
F1 and accuracy differ, especially on imbalanced data.
F1 is a quality metric, not a speed metric.
takeaway: F1 = harmonic mean of precision and recall.

question: A 5-class model performs very well on two common classes and poorly on three rare classes. The business cares equally about every class. Which metric shows this problem MOST clearly?
options: Training loss
Overall accuracy
Micro-averaged F1 score
Macro-averaged F1 score
explanations: Training loss doesn’t show per-class performance.
Accuracy is dominated by the common classes.
Micro averaging weights by sample count, so common classes dominate.
Macro averaging gives each class equal weight, exposing poor rare-class performance.
takeaway: Every class matters equally → macro averaging.

question: Which regression metric describes the share of variance in the target that the model explains, where 1.0 is a perfect fit?
options: Perplexity
Recall
BLEU
R²
explanations: Perplexity evaluates language models.
Recall is a classification metric.
BLEU evaluates translations.
R² measures the proportion of variance explained by the model.
takeaway: R² = explained variance; RMSE/MAE = error size.

question: A document processing model extracts payment amounts. Errors on large payments are costly, so the business wants people to check uncertain results before payment. Which design is MOST appropriate?
options: Route risky cases to people
Lower the model’s temperature to 0
Have people review every document, regardless of confidence
Retrain the model every day
explanations: Human-in-the-loop review focuses people on risky or uncertain cases.
Extraction models may not use temperature, and it doesn’t add review.
Reviewing everything wastes effort on easy cases.
Retraining doesn’t catch individual mistakes before payment.
takeaway: Human-in-the-loop: route low-confidence or high-risk outputs to people.

question: What does a lower perplexity on a held-out text set indicate about a language model?
options: It predicts the text better
Its answers are more factually correct
It has fewer parameters
It generates text faster
explanations: Perplexity measures how well a model predicts a sample; lower is better.
Perplexity doesn’t measure factual accuracy.
Perplexity doesn’t count parameters.
Perplexity isn’t a speed measure.
takeaway: Perplexity = how well a model predicts text (lower is better), not correctness.

question: A company wants every assistant answer scored on whether it follows its refund policy rubric, which none of the built-in metrics covers. It wants an automated, repeatable score. What should the ML engineer use?
options: A judge-model evaluation with a custom rubric metric
Token counts of each answer compared with a target
BLEU scores against a single reference answer for each question
A content filter in a guardrail on every answer
explanations: Custom metrics let the evaluator model score responses against your own criteria.
Length doesn’t measure compliance.
N-gram overlap can’t judge policy compliance.
Content filters block harmful content, not policy compliance.
takeaway: Business-specific quality criteria → LLM-as-a-judge with custom metrics.

question: A team wants to compare its self-hosted model on SageMaker AI with a Bedrock model using the same judge-based metrics. How can it evaluate the self-hosted model with Bedrock Evaluations?
options: Copy the model weights into the evaluation job
Import the SageMaker endpoint as a Bedrock knowledge base
Bring its own inference responses in the prompt dataset
Bedrock can’t evaluate responses from outside models
explanations: Evaluation jobs don’t take model weights.
Knowledge bases store documents, not models.
Bedrock evaluations can score responses that you supply from any model.
Bring-your-own-response evaluation is supported.
takeaway: Evaluate any model with Bedrock → supply your own inference responses.

question: In a RAG evaluation, retrieved passages are relevant, but answers still include facts that aren’t in those passages. Which metric captures this problem?
options: Faithfulness
Context coverage
Context relevance
Recall@k of the retriever
explanations: Faithfulness measures whether the answer is supported by the retrieved context.
Coverage measures whether retrieval found the needed information.
Relevance measures whether the retrieved passages relate to the question.
Recall@k measures retrieval, not generation.
takeaway: Answers not supported by retrieved context → low faithfulness (fix with prompts, grounding checks).

question: A team uses an LLM judge to compare answers from two models side by side. It notices that the judge prefers whichever answer appears first, regardless of quality. Which change gives a fairer comparison?
options: Raise the judge model’s temperature to 1.0 for more varied scores
Score each pair in both orders and combine the results
Put the newer model’s answer in the first position every time
Use a smaller judge model that runs faster on each comparison
explanations: Random variation doesn’t correct a systematic bias.
Swapping positions cancels out the judge’s preference for the first answer.
This builds the bias into every result instead of removing it.
A smaller judge doesn’t remove the ordering bias and may judge less accurately.
takeaway: LLM judges have biases (position, length, self-preference) → swap orders, use rubrics, spot-check with humans.

question: A scikit-learn model receives a few hundred requests a day in unpredictable bursts, with hours of no traffic in between. Requests can tolerate an occasional delay of a few seconds. The model needs 2 GB of memory and no GPU. Which deployment option is the MOST cost-effective?
options: SageMaker Serverless Inference
A batch transform job that runs every 10 minutes and waits for new requests
A real-time endpoint on an ml.m5.large instance with auto scaling to two instances
A multi-model endpoint on a GPU instance that hosts the model with other models
explanations: Serverless endpoints scale to zero when idle and bill per use; cold starts are acceptable here.
Batch transform is for offline datasets, not on-demand requests.
Real-time endpoints keep at least one instance running and billing during idle hours.
A GPU instance is unnecessary and runs continuously.
takeaway: Spiky, infrequent, CPU-only traffic that tolerates cold starts → serverless inference.

question: A model analyzes uploaded videos of up to 800 MB, and each analysis takes 10–20 minutes. Users are notified when results are ready. The endpoint should cost nothing when there are no uploads. Which inference option should the ML engineer use?
options: Asynchronous inference with an SNS success notification
Real-time inference with a 60-second timeout
A batch transform job that is started for each uploaded video
Serverless inference with the largest memory size
explanations: Async inference queues requests, accepts payloads up to 1 GB, runs up to an hour, and can scale to zero.
Real-time requests can’t carry 800 MB payloads or run for 20 minutes.
Starting a batch job per upload adds startup delay and doesn’t provide an endpoint queue.
Serverless has small payload limits and short timeouts.
takeaway: Large payloads, long processing, scale to zero → asynchronous inference.

question: Every night, a bank scores 40 million accounts for churn risk and writes the results to Amazon S3. No application needs predictions during the day. Which option is the MOST cost-effective?
options: Asynchronous inference with one request per account
A SageMaker AI batch transform job
Serverless inference with 40 million individual requests
A real-time endpoint that runs all day and is invoked overnight
explanations: Async endpoints are for individual queued requests, not bulk datasets.
Batch transform runs on a full dataset and releases the compute when the job ends.
Per-request invocation of a whole dataset is slow and expensive.
A persistent endpoint bills while idle all day.
takeaway: Score a whole dataset on a schedule → batch transform.

question: A team self-hosts an open-weight 8-billion-parameter model for an interactive assistant that needs time-to-first-token under 300 ms and steady traffic all day. Which deployment option is MOST appropriate?
options: An asynchronous endpoint that sends results to an SNS topic
SageMaker Serverless Inference with 6 GB of memory
A batch transform job that runs every minute on new prompts
A real-time GPU endpoint with an LMI container
explanations: Async inference queues requests and doesn’t suit live chat.
Serverless inference doesn’t support GPUs and has cold starts.
Batch jobs can’t meet interactive latency.
Real-time GPU endpoints with an optimized LMI container serve steady interactive LLM traffic with low latency.
takeaway: Interactive, steady LLM traffic → real-time GPU endpoint (LMI container).

question: A SaaS company trains a separate XGBoost model for each of its 3,000 customers. Each model is small and is called a few times an hour. Hosting one endpoint per model is too expensive. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective?
options: A multi-model endpoint that loads models from Amazon S3 when they’re called
A multi-container endpoint with 3,000 containers
An inference pipeline that runs all 3,000 models in sequence
One serverless endpoint per customer with provisioned concurrency
explanations: Multi-model endpoints share instances across many same-framework models and cache them on demand.
Multi-container endpoints support up to 15 containers, not thousands.
Pipelines chain containers for one request; they don’t host many alternative models.
Provisioned concurrency on 3,000 endpoints adds a constant cost for each one.
takeaway: Many small, same-framework models with sparse traffic → multi-model endpoint.

question: A team must host a TensorFlow model and a PyTorch model that are invoked independently by different applications. Traffic is low, and the team wants to share one endpoint to reduce cost without modifying the models into one container. Which option should the team use?
options: An inference pipeline that runs the TensorFlow model, then the PyTorch model
A multi-model endpoint with both models
Two production variants with 50% traffic each
A multi-container endpoint
explanations: Pipelines run containers in sequence for every request, which these apps don’t need.
Multi-model endpoints require models that use the same serving container.
Variants split traffic between versions; apps can’t choose a framework per request without extra routing.
Multi-container endpoints host different containers on one endpoint and can invoke each one directly.
takeaway: Different frameworks, independent calls, one endpoint → multi-container endpoint (direct invocation).

question: Every prediction request must pass through a scikit-learn feature transformer, then an XGBoost model, and then a post-processing step that formats the result. The team wants one endpoint call per request. Which deployment pattern fits?
options: A multi-model endpoint that hosts the three artifacts
An asynchronous endpoint with three SNS topics
A SageMaker AI inference pipeline with three containers
Three separate endpoints called one after another by the client
explanations: Multi-model endpoints serve one model per request, not a chain.
Async notifications don’t chain processing steps.
An inference pipeline runs up to 15 containers in sequence behind one endpoint call.
This adds network hops and client complexity.
takeaway: Sequential preprocess → model → postprocess in one call → inference pipeline.

question: A team hosts three fine-tuned open-weight models on SageMaker AI. Each needs a different number of GPUs, and traffic for each model varies independently. The team wants to share instances and scale each model separately. Which feature should the team use?
options: Three production variants with fixed traffic weights
Inference components on one shared real-time endpoint
A multi-model endpoint with GPU instances
One serverless endpoint per model
explanations: Variants split one model’s traffic; they don’t isolate resources per model.
Inference components assign accelerators and memory per model and scale each model’s copies independently.
Multi-model endpoints don’t let you allocate GPUs per model or scale models separately.
Serverless inference doesn’t support GPUs.
takeaway: Multiple models sharing GPU instances with per-model resources and scaling → inference components.

question: A company wants to use a foundation model through an API for a document assistant. The team has no infrastructure staff, traffic is unpredictable, and the model is available in Amazon Bedrock. Which deployment option has the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Run the model in Amazon EKS with GPU node groups
Deploy the model from SageMaker JumpStart to a real-time endpoint with auto scaling
Run the model on Amazon EC2 GPU instances behind a load balancer
Invoke the model on demand through the Amazon Bedrock API
explanations: Kubernetes adds significant operational work.
Self-hosting requires choosing instances, scaling policies, and patching containers.
This requires managing servers, drivers, and scaling.
Bedrock is serverless; you pay per token with no infrastructure to manage.
takeaway: Least ops for an available FM → Bedrock on-demand.

question: A team fine-tuned a Llama-architecture model on another platform and has the weights in Hugging Face safetensors format. It wants to serve the model through the same serverless Bedrock APIs that its applications already use. Which solution should the team use?
options: Register the weights in a Bedrock prompt in Prompt Management
Create a Bedrock fine-tuning job that uses the weights as training data
Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import
Upload the weights to a Bedrock knowledge base
explanations: Prompt Management stores prompts, not models.
Fine-tuning jobs take datasets, not finished weights.
Custom Model Import brings supported open architectures from S3 into Bedrock for serverless invocation.
Knowledge bases store documents for retrieval, not model weights.
takeaway: Bring your own fine-tuned open-weight model to Bedrock APIs → Custom Model Import.

question: A data scientist trained a scikit-learn model on a laptop and saved it as model.joblib. The team wants to host it on a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint without building a container. What should the team do?
options: Convert the model into a Bedrock custom model
The prebuilt scikit-learn container
Retrain the model with the SageMaker AI Linear Learner algorithm
Upload model.joblib to Amazon ECR as a container image and point the endpoint at it
explanations: Bedrock imports supported foundation model architectures, not scikit-learn models.
Prebuilt framework containers load your artifact from S3 and run your inference handler.
Retraining isn’t needed to host an existing model.
ECR stores container images, not model files.
takeaway: Model trained elsewhere → artifact in S3 + prebuilt framework container.

question: A team built an agent with the Strands Agents framework. It must serve many users with complete isolation between user sessions, support sessions that run for up to an hour, and require no servers to manage. Which AWS service should the team use to host the agent?
options: AWS Lambda with a 15-minute timeout
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime
A SageMaker AI real-time endpoint
Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group
explanations: Lambda’s 15-minute limit is too short, and session isolation and state must be built yourself.
AgentCore Runtime is serverless, framework-agnostic, isolates each session in its own microVM, and supports long-running sessions.
Endpoints serve model inference, not long-running isolated agent sessions.
EC2 requires managing servers and building session isolation.
takeaway: Serverless, session-isolated hosting for any agent framework → AgentCore Runtime.

question: An agent must call 40 existing internal REST APIs (described with OpenAPI specifications) and several Lambda functions as tools. The team wants the tools exposed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), with authentication handled centrally. Which service should the team use?
options: AWS Step Functions with one state per API
Amazon EventBridge with one rule per API
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
Amazon API Gateway with a usage plan
explanations: Step Functions orchestrates workflows, not agent tool discovery.
EventBridge routes events, not agent tool calls.
AgentCore Gateway converts OpenAPI, Smithy, and Lambda targets into MCP tools and manages inbound and outbound authentication.
API Gateway fronts APIs but doesn’t translate them into MCP tools for agents.
takeaway: Expose APIs and Lambda functions as MCP tools → AgentCore Gateway.

question: A company is building a system in which a planning agent delegates tasks to specialist agents built by other teams, and each agent also calls tools such as databases and search APIs. Which TWO protocols match these interactions? (Select TWO.)
options: OAuth 2.0 token exchange for delegating tasks and passing results between agents
Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol for communication between agents
OpenTelemetry for calling the search and database tools
AG-UI protocol for connecting agents to databases and search tools
Model Context Protocol (MCP) for connecting agents to tools
explanations: OAuth handles authorization; agent-to-agent communication uses A2A.
A2A standardizes how agents discover and exchange tasks with other agents.
OpenTelemetry carries traces and metrics, not tool calls.
AG-UI connects agents to user interfaces; MCP connects agents to tools.
MCP standardizes how agents discover and call tools and data sources.
takeaway: Agent ↔ agent → A2A; agent ↔ tools → MCP.

topic: Shard a large model across GPUs
question: A 70-billion-parameter model doesn’t fit in the memory of a single GPU on an ml.p4d.24xlarge instance, which has 8 GPUs. The team is deploying it to a SageMaker AI endpoint with a large model inference (LMI) container. Which configuration allows the model to load?
options: Set the number of model copies to 8
Set the tensor parallel degree to 8
Switch to serverless inference with 6 GB of memory
Enable data capture on the endpoint
explanations: Each copy still needs to fit on one GPU.
Tensor parallelism shards the model’s weights across GPUs on the instance.
Serverless inference has no GPUs and far too little memory.
Data capture logs requests; it doesn’t affect memory.
takeaway: Model larger than one GPU at inference → tensor parallelism across GPUs.

question: Users ask a Bedrock knowledge base multi-part questions such as “Compare the parental leave policies in Canada and Japan.” Retrieval returns passages about only one country. Which knowledge base configuration should the ML engineer enable?
options: Query decomposition
A larger chunk overlap
A higher temperature for the generation model
A lower number of retrieved results
explanations: Decomposing the question retrieves passages for each part before generating a combined answer.
Overlap doesn’t help retrieve two separate topics.
Temperature affects generation, not retrieval.
Fewer results make it less likely that both countries are covered.
takeaway: Multi-part questions → query decomposition (reformulation) before retrieval.

question: An application calls a Bedrock model at a steady, high rate around the clock and receives throttling errors during peaks. The business needs guaranteed capacity for the model and can commit to a term. Which option should the ML engineer use?
options: The Flex service tier for every request
Provisioned Throughput for the model
Client retries with exponential backoff
Batch inference for all requests
explanations: Flex trades latency for a discount; it doesn’t guarantee capacity.
Provisioned Throughput reserves dedicated model units for consistent capacity.
Retries help with occasional throttling but don’t add capacity.
Batch inference is asynchronous and doesn’t serve live requests.
takeaway: Steady, high volume needing guaranteed capacity → Provisioned Throughput (commitment).

question: An ML platform team uses AWS CloudFormation. A networking stack creates the VPC, subnets, and security groups, and separate stacks create SageMaker AI endpoints that must use those network resources. How should the endpoint stacks reference the network resources without hard-coding IDs?
options: Store the IDs in a text file in Amazon S3 and download it during deployment
Stack outputs with Export, read with Fn::ImportValue
Create the VPC again in every endpoint stack
Copy the subnet IDs into each endpoint template manually
explanations: This adds custom tooling instead of native stack references.
Stack exports and imports pass values between stacks and keep them consistent.
Duplicating network resources creates separate, unconnected VPCs.
Hard-coded IDs break when the network stack changes.
takeaway: Share values between CloudFormation stacks → Outputs with Export + Fn::ImportValue.

question: An ML team prefers to define its SageMaker AI endpoints, IAM roles, and S3 buckets in Python, using loops and classes, and then deploy them as CloudFormation stacks. Which tool should the team use?
options: AWS CDK
AWS Config
AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store
AWS CloudTrail
explanations: The CDK defines infrastructure in programming languages such as Python and synthesizes CloudFormation templates.
Config records and evaluates resource configurations.
Parameter Store stores configuration values.
CloudTrail records API activity.
takeaway: Infrastructure defined in Python that deploys through CloudFormation → AWS CDK.

question: A team builds its own inference container for SageMaker AI. Endpoint creation fails with a health check error. Which requirement is the container MOST likely missing?
options: An Application Load Balancer inside the container
Handlers for GET /ping and POST /invocations on port 8080
An SSH server on port 22 so that SageMaker can run health checks
A cron job that downloads the model every minute
explanations: SageMaker provides the endpoint routing.
SageMaker checks health with /ping and sends inference requests to /invocations on port 8080.
SageMaker doesn’t connect to containers over SSH.
SageMaker copies the model artifact to /opt/ml/model at startup.
takeaway: Custom serving containers: /ping and /invocations on port 8080.

question: An ML team pushes inference images to Amazon ECR with the tag “latest.” A rollback failed because the “latest” tag had already been overwritten by a broken image. Which TWO actions will prevent this in the future? (Select TWO.)
options: Add an ECR lifecycle policy and keep deploying the “latest” tag
Store the images in Amazon S3 instead of ECR
Tag each image with a unique version, such as the Git commit ID, and deploy by that tag
Enable enhanced scanning on the repository
Enable tag immutability on the ECR repository
explanations: Deploying a mutable “latest” tag still lets a broken image replace the one you need for rollback.
SageMaker pulls serving images from ECR.
Unique tags or digests make every deployment reproducible and easy to roll back.
Scanning finds vulnerabilities but doesn’t protect tags.
Immutable tags can’t be overwritten by a later push.
takeaway: Reproducible rollbacks → unique image tags/digests + ECR tag immutability.

question: A SageMaker AI endpoint runs in private subnets with no internet access. The model container must read reference data from Amazon S3, and applications in the same VPC must invoke the endpoint without traffic leaving the AWS network. Which TWO resources should the ML engineer create? (Select TWO.)
options: An S3 gateway VPC endpoint
A public IP address on each endpoint instance
An internet gateway attached to the private subnets
A NAT gateway in each private subnet
An interface VPC endpoint for the SageMaker Runtime API
explanations: A gateway endpoint lets resources in private subnets reach S3 without internet access.
Endpoint instances are managed by SageMaker, and public IPs violate the requirement.
This would expose the subnets to the internet.
The subnets must have no internet access; a gateway endpoint reaches S3 privately.
An interface endpoint (PrivateLink) lets applications call InvokeEndpoint privately.
takeaway: Private endpoints: S3 gateway endpoint + SageMaker Runtime interface endpoint.

question: An ML engineer deploys a model to a real-time endpoint by using the low-level Boto3 SageMaker client. In which order must the engineer call the APIs?
options: CreateEndpointConfig, CreateEndpoint, CreateModel
CreateEndpoint, CreateModel, CreateEndpointConfig
CreateModel, CreateEndpointConfig, CreateEndpoint
CreateTrainingJob, CreateEndpoint, CreateModel
explanations: The endpoint configuration must reference an existing model.
An endpoint needs an existing endpoint configuration.
The model defines the container and artifact, the configuration defines the instances, and the endpoint deploys the configuration.
A training job isn’t required to deploy an existing artifact, and the order is wrong.
takeaway: Boto3 deployment: CreateModel → CreateEndpointConfig → CreateEndpoint.

question: A real-time endpoint serves an LLM that streams tokens. Each request runs for 10–40 seconds. Scaling based on InvocationsPerInstance reacts too slowly to traffic spikes, and requests queue up. Which scaling metric should the ML engineer use?
options: CPUUtilization with a target value of 90% on each instance
Invocation4XXErrors
DiskUtilization
The high-resolution ConcurrentRequestsPerModel metric
explanations: GPU-bound LLM serving often shows low CPU even when the model is saturated.
Client errors don’t indicate load.
Disk use doesn’t track concurrent requests.
It counts in-flight requests every 10 seconds, so scaling reacts faster to long-running streaming requests.
takeaway: Long-running or streaming requests → scale on high-resolution concurrent requests.

question: An image generation model on a GPU endpoint saturates the GPU at moderate request rates, but CPU utilization stays low. Which metric should a custom target tracking policy use to scale the endpoint?
options: GPUUtilization
CPUUtilization
Invocation5XXErrors
ModelSetupTime
explanations: Scaling on GPU utilization tracks the resource that limits throughput.
CPU stays low, so the policy wouldn’t scale out.
Errors are a symptom, not a capacity metric to target.
Setup time doesn’t track load.
takeaway: GPU-bound models → scale on GPUUtilization (custom metric).

question: An ML engineer is creating an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base for HR documents stored in Amazon S3. Which TWO choices must the engineer make when creating it? (Select TWO.)
options: An Amazon EMR cluster size for chunking the documents
An embedding model
A Provisioned Throughput commitment for the embedding model
A vector store, such as Amazon S3 Vectors or OpenSearch Serverless
A SageMaker AI training instance type
explanations: Knowledge bases parse and chunk documents for you during ingestion.
The embedding model converts chunks and queries into vectors.
Embedding calls run on demand by default.
The vector store holds the embeddings for retrieval.
Knowledge bases don’t train models.
takeaway: Knowledge base setup = data source + embedding model + vector store (+ chunking).

question: HR updates documents in the S3 data source of a Bedrock knowledge base several times a day. Employees still receive answers based on old versions. What should the ML engineer do?
options: Increase the number of retrieved results
Switch to a larger embedding model
Sync the data source
Re-create the knowledge base every day from the same S3 data source
explanations: Retrieval still searches the old vectors.
Embedding quality doesn’t fix stale content.
A sync processes added, changed, and deleted documents so the vector store is current.
Re-creating it is unnecessary and disruptive.
takeaway: Changed source documents → run an ingestion job (sync), ideally automated.

question: A team needs full control of the prompt sent to the model: it wants to add retrieved passages, user profile data, and business rules before calling a model of its choice. Which knowledge base API should the application call?
options: The StartIngestionJob API
The InvokeModel API without retrieval
The RetrieveAndGenerate API with default settings
Retrieve, then Converse with its own prompt
explanations: Ingestion jobs sync documents; they don’t answer queries.
Without retrieval, the passages aren’t included.
RetrieveAndGenerate builds the prompt and generates the answer for you, with less control.
Retrieve returns passages so the application can build its own prompt and call any model.
takeaway: Full control of prompt assembly → Retrieve, then call the model yourself.

question: A travel agent built on AgentCore must remember details within a conversation, such as the destination mentioned earlier, and must also remember each user’s seat and meal preferences across future sessions. Which solution meets both requirements with the LEAST custom code?
options: Store the full conversation history in the system prompt of every request
AgentCore Memory (short-term and long-term)
An Amazon ElastiCache cluster with a 5-minute TTL
Model fine-tuning on each user’s conversations every night
explanations: This grows prompts and doesn’t extract preferences across sessions.
Short-term memory keeps turn-by-turn context; long-term memory extracts preferences and facts across sessions.
A short TTL loses preferences between sessions, and extraction must be coded.
Fine-tuning per user is impractical and slow.
takeaway: Within-session context + cross-session preferences → AgentCore Memory (short- and long-term).

question: An agent hosted on AgentCore Runtime must create tickets in a third-party SaaS tool on behalf of each signed-in user, using OAuth tokens. The team doesn’t want to store user tokens in the agent code. Which capability should the team use?
options: Hard-coded API keys in environment variables
IAM roles with a trust policy for the SaaS provider
AWS Secrets Manager with one shared secret for all users
AgentCore Identity for outbound OAuth credential management
explanations: This is insecure and isn’t per user.
IAM roles authorize AWS access, not access to external SaaS APIs.
A shared secret doesn’t act on behalf of each user.
AgentCore Identity handles OAuth flows and securely stores and supplies per-user tokens to the agent.
takeaway: Agents acting on behalf of users in third-party apps → AgentCore Identity (outbound OAuth).

question: A team is deploying a customer service agent that must run serverlessly, call internal APIs as tools, remember customers across sessions, and send traces to CloudWatch. Which combination of AgentCore components meets these requirements?
options: Runtime and Code Interpreter
Code Interpreter, Browser, Policy, and Evaluations
Gateway and Browser
Runtime, Gateway, Memory, and Observability
explanations: This combination lacks API tools and long-term memory.
These provide code execution, web browsing, tool-call authorization, and quality scoring, not hosting, tools, and memory.
There’s no hosting or memory in this combination.
Runtime hosts the agent, Gateway exposes APIs as tools, Memory keeps customer context, and Observability sends traces.
takeaway: Host → Runtime; tools → Gateway; memory → Memory; traces → Observability.

question: A team wants to update a SageMaker AI endpoint to a new model version by first sending 10% of traffic to the new version for 15 minutes and rolling back automatically if latency or error alarms fire. Which deployment configuration should the team use?
options: Delete the endpoint and create a new one with the new model
Add the new model as a second production variant with 0% traffic
A rolling deployment with a batch size of 100%
Blue/green with canary traffic shifting and automatic alarm-based rollback
explanations: This causes downtime and has no rollback.
A 0% variant receives no traffic to test.
This replaces all capacity at once and doesn’t test a canary first.
Canary shifting sends a small share first, bakes, and rolls back if alarms fire.
takeaway: Small first step + bake + automatic rollback → blue/green canary with alarms.

question: A team wants to shift traffic to a new endpoint version in five equal steps of 20%, monitoring alarms after each step. Which traffic shifting mode should the team choose?
options: Shadow
Linear
All at once
Canary
explanations: Shadow testing doesn’t serve the new version’s responses.
Linear shifting moves traffic in equal, configurable steps with baking periods.
All-at-once shifts 100% in one step.
Canary uses two steps: a small canary, then the rest.
takeaway: N equal steps → linear traffic shifting.

question: An endpoint runs on 20 expensive GPU instances. A blue/green update would temporarily require 40 instances, which exceeds the account’s instance quota. The team still wants gradual updates with automatic rollback. Which deployment option should the team use?
options: Blue/green with all-at-once traffic shifting
A rolling deployment in 25% batches with CloudWatch alarms
A multi-model endpoint that loads the new model version on demand
Shadow testing for every update
explanations: Blue/green still provisions a full green fleet.
Rolling deployments update capacity in batches, so they don’t double the fleet, and they can roll back on alarms.
Multi-model endpoints don’t change how updates are rolled out.
Shadow tests evaluate a variant; they don’t replace the production model.
takeaway: Avoid doubling capacity during updates → rolling deployment.

question: An ML team stores its training code in GitHub. On every merge to the main branch, it wants AWS to run unit tests, build a container image, and push it to Amazon ECR. Which combination of services should the team use?
options: Amazon EventBridge with an Amazon SQS queue
AWS CodeArtifact with a scheduled AWS Lambda function
AWS CodePipeline with an AWS CodeConnections source and an AWS CodeBuild stage
AWS CodeDeploy triggered by an Amazon S3 event
explanations: Event routing alone doesn’t build or test code.
CodeArtifact stores packages; it doesn’t run builds.
CodeConnections links GitHub to CodePipeline, and CodeBuild runs tests and builds and pushes the image.
CodeDeploy deploys applications; it doesn’t build images from GitHub merges.
takeaway: GitHub → CodeConnections → CodePipeline → CodeBuild (tests, image build, push).

question: A CodeBuild project builds an inference image successfully but fails at the docker push step with an “AccessDenied” error for Amazon ECR. What should the ML engineer fix?
options: Increase the compute type of the CodeBuild project
Enable privileged mode on the CodeBuild project
Fix the CodeBuild service role
Move the buildspec file to the repository root and rename it buildspec.yml
explanations: Compute size doesn’t affect ECR permissions.
Privileged mode is needed to build Docker images, and the build already works, so it isn’t the cause.
The service role must allow authenticating to ECR and uploading image layers.
The buildspec already runs; the failure is an authorization error.
takeaway: CodeBuild AccessDenied on ECR → fix the CodeBuild service role permissions.

question: A new training job that uses ml.p4d.24xlarge fails immediately with a ResourceLimitExceeded error. Other training jobs that use ml.m5.xlarge run normally. What should the ML engineer do?
options: Enable managed spot training
Add a VPC configuration with private subnets to the training job
Lower the max_run value of the job
Raise the instance quota
explanations: Spot training still needs available quota for the instance type.
Networking doesn’t affect instance quotas.
The run time isn’t the limiting factor.
Each instance type has a per-account quota, which can be 0 until you request an increase.
takeaway: ResourceLimitExceeded for an instance type → raise that SageMaker quota.

question: A SageMaker Pipelines workflow trains and evaluates a model each week. The team wants the pipeline to register the model only if its F1 score on the test set is at least 0.85; otherwise, it should stop with a failure message. Which steps should the team add?
options: A Transform step that scores the test set again
A Lambda step that deletes models with low scores after registration
A Callback step that waits for manual review of every model
A Condition step that compares the F1 score, followed by a model registration step or a Fail step
explanations: Scoring again doesn’t decide whether to register.
Registering first and deleting later isn’t a gate.
Manual review isn’t needed for a numeric threshold.
Condition steps branch on evaluation metrics, so only passing models are registered.
takeaway: Metric threshold gate in Pipelines → Condition step → register or Fail.

question: A team wants its SageMaker AI retraining pipeline to start automatically every Sunday and also whenever a drift-detection job publishes a CloudWatch alarm in the ALARM state. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST custom code?
options: An AWS Glue trigger that runs the pipeline
A SageMaker Studio notebook that a team member runs on Sundays
A cron job on an EC2 instance that polls CloudWatch every minute
EventBridge schedule and alarm rules that start the pipeline
explanations: Glue triggers start Glue jobs and crawlers, not SageMaker pipelines.
Manual runs aren’t automated.
This requires managing a server and polling code.
EventBridge can start a SageMaker pipeline directly from schedules and from CloudWatch alarm events.
takeaway: Scheduled or event-driven retraining → EventBridge rules that start the pipeline.

question: Models are registered in SageMaker Model Registry with the status PendingManualApproval. When a reviewer changes a model’s status to Approved, a deployment pipeline must start automatically. How should the ML engineer implement this?
options: Poll the model registry every hour with a Lambda function
An EventBridge rule on the model package state change event type
Use an S3 event notification on the model artifact
Ask reviewers to start the deployment manually after approval
explanations: Polling adds delay and custom code.
Model Registry emits events when approval status changes, which EventBridge can route to CodePipeline or a pipeline.
The artifact doesn’t change when the approval status does.
Manual starts aren’t automated.
takeaway: Approval in Model Registry → EventBridge event → deployment pipeline.

question: Auditors ask which training data, code version, and metrics produced each model that was deployed in the last year, and who approved it. Which approach meets this requirement?
options: Register each version in SageMaker Model Registry
Keep the latest model artifact in S3 and overwrite older ones
Store a spreadsheet of model versions in Amazon S3
Use CloudWatch Logs retention of 30 days
explanations: Model Registry versions models in groups and records metrics, lineage, and approval history.
Older versions would be lost.
Manual records are error-prone and aren’t linked to artifacts.
Logs expire and don’t describe model lineage.
takeaway: Model versioning for audits → Model Registry (versions, metrics, lineage, approvals).

question: Developers iterate on a prompt in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management. Production applications must keep using a tested prompt until a new one is approved. How should the applications reference the prompt?
options: By the prompt name in an environment variable that developers edit
By the ARN of a specific prompt version
By copying the prompt text into the application code
By the prompt’s draft identifier
explanations: Editing a name doesn’t pin a tested version.
Prompt versions are immutable snapshots, so production stays on the tested prompt.
Copies drift from the managed prompt and need code deploys to change.
The draft changes as developers edit it.
takeaway: Pin production to an immutable prompt version.

question: A team deploys an agent with AgentCore Runtime. Every code update creates a new runtime version. Production traffic must stay on the tested version until the team explicitly promotes the next one. How should the team configure production?
options: Pin a production endpoint to a version; update it to promote
Redeploy the agent as a new runtime for each release
Point production clients at the DEFAULT endpoint of the agent runtime
Delete old versions after each update
explanations: Custom endpoints stay on their version until you update them explicitly.
This changes the runtime identity instead of using versions and endpoints.
DEFAULT moves to the latest version automatically after every update.
Versions are immutable and are the rollback targets.
takeaway: AgentCore: DEFAULT tracks latest; pin prod with a named endpoint on a version.

question: Before promoting a new prompt version to production, a team wants its CI/CD pipeline to check automatically that answers to 300 golden questions haven’t become less correct. Which approach should the team add to the pipeline?
options: A manual review of five random answers
A CodeBuild step that checks the prompt for spelling errors
Run a Bedrock evaluation on the golden set and fail below a threshold
A load test that measures latency and throttling at peak production traffic
explanations: A small manual sample isn’t automated or thorough.
Spelling checks don’t measure answer quality.
Automated evaluation against a fixed test set catches regressions before promotion.
Latency tests don’t measure correctness.
takeaway: Prompt CI → automated evaluation on a golden set with a pass/fail threshold.

question: Documents for a Bedrock knowledge base are produced by a nightly ETL job. The team wants the knowledge base to sync only after the ETL job succeeds, and to notify the team if the sync fails. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Configure S3 Lifecycle rules on the data source bucket
Ask users to report when answers look outdated
A Step Functions workflow: ETL job, then sync, with an SNS alert on any failure
Run the ingestion job on a fixed schedule one hour after the ETL job starts
explanations: Lifecycle rules move or expire objects; they don’t sync knowledge bases.
This isn’t automated.
Step Functions sequences the steps, waits for success, and handles failures.
A fixed schedule can sync before the ETL job finishes.
takeaway: Sequenced data refresh with error handling → Step Functions orchestration.

question: A SageMaker Pipelines workflow reruns a 2-hour data processing step even when its inputs and code haven’t changed, which delays experiments. Which feature should the ML engineer enable?
options: Step caching for the processing step
Managed spot training for the processing step
A Callback step before the processing step
Warm pools for the training step
explanations: Caching reuses a previous successful run when the step’s inputs and configuration are unchanged.
Spot capacity lowers cost but still reruns the step.
Callbacks wait for external signals.
Warm pools reduce startup time for training jobs, not processing reruns.
takeaway: Avoid rerunning unchanged steps → Pipelines step caching.

question: A company already runs hundreds of Apache Airflow DAGs for data engineering and wants to add ML training and deployment tasks to the same DAGs with minimal change to its tooling. Which service should it use?
options: SageMaker Pipelines
Amazon MWAA
AWS Glue workflows
Amazon EventBridge Scheduler
explanations: Pipelines is ML-native but would introduce a second orchestration tool.
MWAA runs existing Airflow DAGs as a managed service, and Airflow has SageMaker operators.
Glue workflows orchestrate Glue jobs and crawlers.
Scheduler starts targets on a schedule but doesn’t run DAGs.
takeaway: Existing Airflow DAGs → Amazon MWAA.

question: An ML engineer runs dozens of short SageMaker AI training jobs in a row while adjusting code. Each job spends several minutes provisioning instances and pulling the container before training starts. Which feature will reduce this startup time for consecutive jobs?
options: A larger instance type for every training job in the series
Managed spot training with a long maximum wait time
SageMaker AI managed warm pools with a keep-alive period
Pipe input mode for all training channels
explanations: Bigger instances don’t remove provisioning time.
Spot capacity lowers cost but can add waiting time.
Warm pools keep instances provisioned after a job ends so the next matching job starts faster.
Pipe mode changes data loading, not instance provisioning.
takeaway: Many back-to-back training jobs → warm pools (KeepAlivePeriodInSeconds).

question: A 15 MB scikit-learn model must score a few requests per minute behind an existing API Gateway REST API. Cold starts of a second are acceptable, and the team wants the fewest AWS services to manage. Which option fits BEST?
options: A SageMaker AI batch transform job triggered for each request
A SageMaker AI real-time endpoint on two ml.m5.xlarge instances
An AWS Lambda function that loads the model and scores each request
An Amazon EKS cluster with a model-serving deployment
explanations: Batch jobs take minutes to start and aren’t meant for single requests.
Two always-on instances are heavy for a tiny, low-traffic model.
A small model fits in a Lambda package or container image and scales to zero with the API.
A Kubernetes cluster adds a lot of operational work for one small model.
takeaway: Tiny models with light traffic can run in Lambda; larger or GPU models → SageMaker AI.

question: A company serves 800 small PyTorch models, one per store, each called a few times an hour. The models need a GPU for acceptable latency. Which option is the MOST cost-effective?
options: A GPU multi-model endpoint
An inference pipeline that chains all 800 models
800 separate real-time endpoints on GPU instances
A serverless endpoint for each model
explanations: GPU multi-model endpoints share GPU instances across many models and cache the active ones.
Pipelines run models in sequence, which this workload doesn’t need.
One GPU endpoint per model is very expensive.
Serverless inference doesn’t support GPUs.
takeaway: Many same-framework models needing GPUs → GPU multi-model endpoint.

question: Which statement correctly describes the difference between an inference pipeline and a multi-container endpoint with direct invocation?
options: Multi-container endpoints require all containers to use the same framework
Inference pipelines can host thousands of models loaded from S3
Pipelines run containers in sequence; direct calls pick one
Both run every container for every request
explanations: Different frameworks are the main reason to use them.
That describes multi-model endpoints.
Pipelines chain processing steps, while direct invocation picks one container per request.
Direct invocation targets one container per request.
takeaway: Inference pipeline = serial chain; multi-container (direct) = pick a container per request.

question: Users of a chat application on a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint wait several seconds before any text appears. The model generates text token by token. What should the ML engineer use so that text appears as it is generated?
options: A larger maximum payload size on the endpoint
Response streaming from the endpoint
Batch transform for each chat message
Asynchronous inference with SNS notifications
explanations: Payload size doesn’t change when tokens are returned.
Streaming returns tokens as they are generated, which reduces perceived latency.
Batch jobs are for offline datasets.
Async inference returns results later through S3.
takeaway: Perceived latency for LLMs → response streaming.

question: A document classification model receives large bursts of uploads a few times a week and must cost nothing between bursts. Each request takes about 2 minutes, and results can arrive later. Which deployment option fits?
options: A real-time endpoint with a minimum of one instance
Serverless inference with 6 GB memory
A multi-container endpoint with direct invocation
Async inference that scales down to zero
explanations: A minimum instance bills between bursts.
Serverless timeouts are too short for 2-minute requests.
This doesn’t queue bursts or scale to zero.
Async endpoints queue bursts and can scale to zero when the queue is empty.
takeaway: Queued bursts, long processing, zero idle cost → async inference (scale to zero).

topic: Specialized model not in the catalog
question: A team needs a domain-specific model that isn’t available as a serverless Bedrock model but is listed in Amazon Bedrock Marketplace. It wants to call it through the same Bedrock APIs as its other models. What should it do?
options: Fine-tune a serverless Bedrock model to imitate it
Deploy it from Bedrock Marketplace to a managed endpoint
Request the model through AWS Support
Import it with Custom Model Import from the Marketplace listing
explanations: Fine-tuning another model doesn’t give access to the specialized one.
Marketplace models run on SageMaker AI–managed endpoints that you size, and they are called through Bedrock APIs.
Support doesn’t add models to accounts.
Custom Model Import is for your own weights in supported architectures.
takeaway: Specialized third-party models → Bedrock Marketplace (endpoint you size and pay for).

question: A bank must run an open-weight model inside its own VPC, choose the exact GPU instance type, and keep model weights in its account. Which deployment option meets these requirements?
options: Deploy it with SageMaker JumpStart into an endpoint in the bank’s VPC
Bedrock batch inference with a VPC endpoint
Prompt routing between two Bedrock models
Amazon Bedrock on-demand inference in the bank’s Region
explanations: JumpStart deploys open models to SageMaker AI endpoints in your account and VPC on instances you choose.
Batch inference is still serverless and is for offline jobs.
Routing chooses models; it doesn’t give infrastructure control.
Serverless Bedrock doesn’t let you choose instances or hold weights in your account.
takeaway: Full control of instances, network, and weights → self-host on SageMaker AI.

question: A team fine-tuned an Amazon Nova model in Amazon Bedrock. Traffic is light and unpredictable, and buying Provisioned Throughput would be wasteful. How should the team serve the custom model?
options: Call the base model and include the fine-tuning data in each prompt
Create a custom model deployment for on-demand inference
Export the weights and host them on a GPU endpoint
Use batch inference for each live request
explanations: This defeats the purpose of fine-tuning and raises costs.
Supported custom models can be deployed for pay-per-use on-demand inference.
Custom Nova weights aren’t exported for self-hosting.
Batch inference is asynchronous and unsuited to live requests.
takeaway: Light traffic on a supported custom model → on-demand custom model deployment.

question: A team fine-tuned a Hugging Face text classification model outside AWS and wants to serve it on SageMaker AI without writing a serving stack. What is the simplest approach?
options: Convert the model to an XGBoost model first
The Hugging Face inference container
Write a Flask server and build a custom container from scratch
Upload the model files to a knowledge base
explanations: Conversion isn’t possible or needed.
The prebuilt Hugging Face container serves supported models from an S3 artifact.
Building a serving stack is unnecessary work.
Knowledge bases hold documents, not models.
takeaway: External Hugging Face models → SageMaker Hugging Face DLC (or import supported FMs into Bedrock).

topic: Host tools as an MCP server
question: A team built an MCP server that exposes internal search tools. It wants to host the server serverlessly with session isolation so that several agents can use it. Which service should host it?
options: Amazon API Gateway with a usage plan
Amazon SageMaker AI batch transform
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime
AWS Step Functions Express workflows
explanations: API Gateway fronts HTTP APIs but doesn’t host MCP server code.
Batch transform runs offline inference jobs.
AgentCore Runtime hosts agents and MCP servers serverlessly with session isolation.
Step Functions orchestrates workflows, not MCP servers.
takeaway: Host agents or MCP servers serverlessly → AgentCore Runtime.

question: A travel company wants one agent to understand the customer’s request and delegate subtasks to specialist agents for flights, hotels, and payments, then combine their results. Which pattern is this?
options: A supervisor agent with specialist sub-agents
A single agent with no tools and a very long prompt
A knowledge base with hierarchical chunking
A batch inference job that runs each agent nightly
explanations: A supervisor plans the task, delegates to specialists, and combines their outputs.
This doesn’t delegate work or integrate specialist systems.
Chunking organizes documents, not agents.
Batch jobs can’t handle interactive requests.
takeaway: Delegating to specialists → supervisor / multi-agent collaboration (A2A between agents).

question: An analytics agent writes Python code to analyze uploaded CSV files. Security requires that the generated code never runs on the agent’s host and has no access to other users’ data. Which capability should the team use?
options: Run the code on a shared EC2 instance with a restricted user
Run the code in the user’s browser through the web app
Run the code in the Lambda function that hosts the agent tools
AgentCore Code Interpreter sandboxes
explanations: A shared host mixes users’ sessions and data.
Client-side execution can’t safely access server-side files or be governed.
Running generated code next to your tools risks data exposure.
Code Interpreter runs code in isolated sandboxes per session.
takeaway: Agents executing code → sandboxed AgentCore Code Interpreter.

topic: Fit an LLM on smaller GPUs
question: A 13-billion-parameter model in 16-bit precision needs about 26 GB for its weights. The team’s budget allows only a single 24 GB GPU per instance. Quality tests show that 8-bit weights are acceptable. Which change allows the model to fit?
options: Use a longer maximum context length
Increase the batch size
Quantize the weights to 8-bit
Enable data capture on the endpoint
explanations: Longer contexts need more KV-cache memory.
Larger batches need more memory.
Halving the bytes per parameter cuts weight memory to about 13 GB.
Data capture doesn’t change memory use.
takeaway: Model memory ≈ parameters × bytes per parameter → quantize to fit smaller GPUs.

question: With inference components, how does an ML engineer control how many GPUs each model uses and how many copies run?
options: By setting per-copy resources and a copy count
By setting the multi-model endpoint cache size
By tagging each model with the number of GPUs it needs
By creating one endpoint configuration per GPU
explanations: Each component declares accelerators, CPU, and memory per copy, and scales its copy count.
Cache size applies to multi-model endpoints, not inference components.
Tags don’t allocate resources.
This isn’t how inference components allocate resources.
takeaway: Inference components: per-copy resource requirements + copy count (auto scaled).

question: A knowledge base answers policy questions. Answers are often diluted by loosely related passages. Which TWO configuration changes are MOST likely to help? (Select TWO.)
options: Increase the number of retrieved passages from 5 to 25 and send all of them to the model
Raise the generation temperature so answers draw on more of the passages
Apply metadata filters, such as department or policy type
Embed queries with a different model than documents
Retrieve a larger candidate set and rerank it down to a few passages
explanations: More loosely related passages make answers more diluted, not less.
Temperature adds randomness; it doesn’t remove loosely related passages.
Filters remove passages from irrelevant document groups.
Mismatched embeddings break retrieval.
Reranking keeps the most relevant passages and drops loosely related ones.
takeaway: Diluted context → rerank to fewer, better passages and filter by metadata.

question: A serverless endpoint serves a model whose traffic jumps every weekday at 09:00 for one hour. Cold starts at 09:00 cause slow responses. Which feature fixes this while keeping serverless pricing for the rest of the day?
options: Send a request every second all day to keep it warm
Provisioned concurrency scheduled for the morning peak
Increase the endpoint’s memory to 6 GB permanently
Switch to a real-time endpoint with four instances all day
explanations: Keep-alive traffic adds cost and isn’t reliable.
Provisioned concurrency keeps capacity warm; Application Auto Scaling can schedule it.
More memory doesn’t remove cold starts.
This pays for instances all day.
takeaway: Predictable bursts on serverless → (scheduled) provisioned concurrency.

question: A team is prototyping with several Bedrock models and sends a few hundred requests a day. Which capacity option is MOST appropriate?
options: Reserved tier capacity through the account team
On-demand inference, paying per token
A dedicated GPU endpoint for each model
Provisioned Throughput with a 6-month commitment
explanations: Reserved capacity is for mission-critical, steady workloads.
Pay-per-token suits low, variable usage.
Self-hosting is unnecessary for prototypes.
Long commitments waste money during prototyping.
takeaway: Low or exploratory usage → on demand.

question: Before updating a CloudFormation stack that holds a production SageMaker AI endpoint, the team wants to see exactly which resources will be replaced. What should it use?
options: Termination protection
A change set
Stack drift detection
Stack outputs
explanations: This prevents stack deletion, not previewing updates.
Change sets show which resources will be added, modified, or replaced before you apply them.
Drift detection shows manual changes since deployment.
Outputs export values; they don’t preview changes.
takeaway: Preview stack updates → change sets; detect manual edits → drift detection.

question: A platform team wants every ML team to create SageMaker AI endpoints with the same encryption, VPC, tags, and alarms, without copying templates. The teams already write infrastructure in Python. What should the platform team provide?
options: A wiki page with screenshots of the console steps
A reusable AWS CDK construct that teams import
A Lambda function that copies existing endpoints
A shared IAM user that creates all endpoints
explanations: Manual steps lead to inconsistent resources.
A construct packages a secure endpoint pattern that teams reuse in their CDK apps.
Copying endpoints doesn’t enforce a standard pattern.
Shared users break least privilege and accountability.
takeaway: Reusable infrastructure patterns in code → CDK constructs (or Service Catalog products).

question: A PyTorch inference script needs one extra system library that isn’t in the AWS Deep Learning Container. The team wants to keep AWS patches and optimizations. What should it do?
options: Install the library at the start of every request
Build a new image from a plain Ubuntu base
Extend the DLC with a Dockerfile that adds it
Switch the model to a built-in algorithm
explanations: Per-request installs slow inference badly.
Starting from scratch loses the optimized framework stack.
Extending a DLC keeps AWS’s framework setup while adding what you need.
Rewriting the model is unnecessary.
takeaway: Missing system dependency → extend the prebuilt DLC (requirements.txt for Python packages).

question: An ECR repository holds thousands of old training images, and storage costs are rising. Which feature removes old images automatically while keeping the most recent ones?
options: Tag immutability on the repository
An ECR lifecycle policy
Enhanced scanning with Inspector
A pull through cache rule
explanations: Immutability prevents overwriting tags; it doesn’t delete images.
Lifecycle policies expire images by age or count.
Scanning finds vulnerabilities.
Pull through cache copies images from upstream registries.
takeaway: Old images piling up → ECR lifecycle policy.

question: Lambda functions in private subnets with no NAT gateway must call the Bedrock runtime API. The traffic must not leave the AWS network. What should the ML engineer create?
options: A VPC peering connection to the Bedrock service VPC
An internet gateway on the private subnets
An interface VPC endpoint for the Bedrock runtime
A gateway VPC endpoint for Bedrock
explanations: You can’t peer with service VPCs.
This would expose the subnets to the internet.
An interface endpoint (PrivateLink) gives private access to the Bedrock runtime API.
Gateway endpoints exist for S3 and DynamoDB only.
takeaway: Private access to Bedrock → interface VPC endpoint (bedrock-runtime).

topic: Training job in a VPC hangs
question: A training job configured with private subnets and no NAT gateway hangs while downloading its input data from Amazon S3, then fails. The same job works without the VPC configuration. What is the MOST likely fix?
options: Enable network isolation on the job
Increase the training instance size
Switch the input mode from File to Pipe
An S3 gateway VPC endpoint
explanations: Isolation removes container network access but SageMaker still needs a path to S3 in your VPC.
Instance size doesn’t create a network path to S3.
Every input mode still needs a network path to S3.
A gateway endpoint lets the job reach S3 from private subnets.
takeaway: Jobs in private subnets need VPC endpoints (S3 gateway; interface endpoints for other APIs).

question: An ML engineer has a new model version and wants to switch a live endpoint to it without downtime by using the SageMaker API. Which sequence is correct?
options: Delete the endpoint, then create a new one with the same name
New model and endpoint config, then UpdateEndpoint
Edit the existing endpoint configuration in place
Upload the new artifact over the old one in S3
explanations: Deleting the endpoint causes downtime.
UpdateEndpoint switches to a new configuration while the endpoint keeps serving.
Endpoint configurations are immutable.
Running instances don’t reload artifacts automatically.
takeaway: Zero-downtime model updates → new EndpointConfig + UpdateEndpoint (with deployment guardrails).

question: A real-time endpoint needs four instances every day between 18:00 and 22:00 and one instance otherwise. Target tracking reacts too late at 18:00. What should the ML engineer add?
options: Response streaming for every request
Scheduled scaling actions for the evening peak
A second endpoint in another Region for the peak
A larger instance type for the endpoint all day
explanations: Streaming doesn’t add capacity.
Scheduled actions raise capacity before a known peak.
Another Region doesn’t solve a predictable local peak.
This pays for unneeded capacity all day.
takeaway: Predictable peaks → scheduled scaling (plus target tracking for the rest).

question: An endpoint hosts several models as inference components. One model is used only during business hours. How can its GPU capacity be released at night while the other models keep running?
options: Reduce the endpoint’s maximum payload size
Move the model to a serverless endpoint with GPUs
Delete the endpoint every evening and recreate it every morning
Allow its inference component to scale to zero copies
explanations: Payload limits don’t release capacity.
Serverless inference doesn’t offer GPUs.
This disrupts the other models.
Inference components can scale a single model to zero while others keep serving.
takeaway: Per-model scale to zero on a shared endpoint → inference components.

topic: Crawl a website into a knowledge base
question: A team wants a Bedrock knowledge base to answer questions from its public documentation website without exporting pages manually. Which data source should it configure?
options: An Amazon Kinesis data stream
An S3 bucket filled with screenshots of the pages
The web crawler data source
An Amazon Redshift structured data store
explanations: Streams aren’t knowledge base data sources.
Screenshots lose the text structure and need manual work.
The web crawler connector ingests pages from the URLs you allow.
Structured stores are for tables, not web pages.
takeaway: Knowledge base data sources include S3, web crawler, Confluence, SharePoint, Salesforce, and custom.

question: A support system creates a few new troubleshooting articles every hour and wants each one searchable within a minute, without running a full data source sync. Which approach fits?
options: Store new articles in the system prompt
The direct document ingestion API
Increase the number of retrieved results
Recreate the vector store every hour
explanations: Prompts grow without limit and aren’t searchable.
Direct ingestion adds or updates specific documents without a full sync.
Retrieval can’t find documents that aren’t indexed.
Recreating the store is slow and wasteful.
takeaway: Fast per-document updates → direct document ingestion; bulk changes → sync jobs.

question: A team builds its own retrieval pipeline: it calls the knowledge base Retrieve API, then must keep only passages from documents the user is allowed to see, and send the best five to the model. Which TWO steps belong in this pipeline? (Select TWO.)
options: Rerank the filtered passages and keep the top five
Filter restricted content out of the generated answer afterward
Send every retrieved passage to the model regardless of permissions
Embed the user’s ID as part of the query text
Apply metadata filters for the user’s permissions in the Retrieve request
explanations: Reranking chooses the most relevant passages to send.
By then restricted passages have already reached the model; filter before generation.
This can leak documents to the wrong users.
User IDs in the query don’t enforce access control.
Filtering at retrieval keeps unauthorized documents out of the results.
takeaway: Custom retrieval: filter (including access) → rerank → assemble prompt.

question: An agent built on AgentCore Memory serves thousands of users. Each user’s long-term preferences must never appear in another user’s session. How should the agent store and read memories?
options: Use a separate actor ID or namespace for each user
Turn off long-term memory and ask users to repeat themselves
Store preferences in the system prompt for all users
Put every user’s preferences in one shared memory record
explanations: Scoping memory records by user keeps each user’s memories separate.
This loses the personalization requirement.
This exposes every user’s data to everyone.
Shared records mix users’ data.
takeaway: Agent memory: scope by user/actor and session.

question: A team runs a custom agent on Amazon ECS and needs to persist conversation state between requests with single-digit millisecond reads, keyed by session ID. Which store is the BEST fit?
options: DynamoDB keyed by session ID
Amazon S3 with one JSON object per message
Amazon CloudWatch Logs streams per session
Amazon Redshift tables keyed by session
explanations: DynamoDB provides fast key-value reads and writes for session state.
S3 works for archives but adds latency and request overhead for state.
Logs aren’t a state store.
A data warehouse is unsuited to low-latency state.
takeaway: Custom agent state → DynamoDB (or AgentCore Memory when on AgentCore).

question: A team plans a 3-week fine-tuning run next month on many GPU instances and is worried that on-demand GPU capacity won’t be available. What should it use?
options: A SageMaker AI training plan reservation
Managed spot training
A larger maximum run time on each job
Serverless inference
explanations: Training plans reserve accelerated capacity for a planned time window.
Spot capacity can be interrupted and isn’t guaranteed.
Run time doesn’t secure capacity.
Serverless inference is for hosting, not training.
takeaway: Guaranteed GPU capacity for planned training → training plans (capacity reservations).

topic: Restrict what an agent may do
question: A support agent can call a refund tool. Compliance requires that refunds above $500 are never executed by the agent, even if the model is manipulated by a prompt. Which control is MOST reliable?
options: Lower the model’s temperature
Enforce the limit outside the model (tool checks or Policy)
Tell the model in the system prompt to stay under $500
Log every refund and have compliance review the logs weekly
explanations: Temperature doesn’t enforce business rules.
Deterministic checks outside the model can’t be talked around.
Prompts can be overridden by prompt injection.
Logging detects violations after the fact.
takeaway: Enforce agent permissions outside the model (tool-side checks, AgentCore Policy).

question: During a canary deployment of a new endpoint version, what causes SageMaker AI to roll back automatically?
options: A manual approval step in the CodePipeline release
A new commit in the source repository
Any change in the model artifact size
A CloudWatch alarm entering ALARM during baking
explanations: Approvals gate releases; they aren’t rollback triggers in deployment guardrails.
Commits don’t affect an in-progress deployment.
Artifact size isn’t monitored for rollback.
Deployment guardrails watch the alarms you specify and roll back if any fire.
takeaway: Guardrail rollbacks are driven by your CloudWatch alarms during baking periods.

question: A Lambda function wraps model inference. The team wants to shift 10% of traffic to a new function version for 10 minutes before moving the rest, rolling back on alarms. Which service provides this?
options: AWS CodeDeploy
AWS CodeArtifact
Amazon ECR
AWS Config
explanations: CodeDeploy shifts Lambda alias traffic with canary or linear configurations and rolls back on alarms.
CodeArtifact stores packages.
ECR stores container images.
Config evaluates resource configurations.
takeaway: Lambda/ECS gradual releases → CodeDeploy; SageMaker endpoints → deployment guardrails.

question: Training jobs and CodeBuild projects run in private subnets and must install the company’s internal Python packages plus approved PyPI packages, without internet access. Which service should the team use?
options: Amazon S3 Glacier
AWS CodeCommit
AWS CodeArtifact
Amazon ECR
explanations: Archive storage can’t serve pip installs.
CodeCommit stores source code, not built packages.
CodeArtifact hosts private packages and caches approved public ones for pip.
ECR stores container images, not pip packages.
takeaway: Private and proxied pip packages → CodeArtifact.

question: An ML team keeps its code in GitLab and wants CodePipeline to start on every merge. Which service connects CodePipeline to GitLab?
options: Amazon EventBridge Scheduler
AWS CodeConnections
AWS CodeCommit
AWS Direct Connect
explanations: Schedules run on time, not on merges.
CodeConnections links CodePipeline to GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket.
CodeCommit is AWS’s own Git service.
Direct Connect is a private network link.
takeaway: Third-party Git sources → CodeConnections.

question: A security review requires that every training job encrypts its storage volume and output with the team’s KMS key and runs in private subnets. Which TWO estimator settings implement this? (Select TWO.)
options: enable_network_isolation set to True, which also places the job in private subnets
subnets and security_group_ids for the private subnets
A larger instance_count
encrypt_inter_container_traffic set to True for the storage volume
volume_kms_key and output_kms_key set to the team’s key
explanations: Network isolation blocks the container’s network calls; it doesn’t choose subnets or encrypt volumes.
The VPC configuration places the job in the approved network.
Instance count doesn’t affect encryption or networking.
This encrypts traffic between training nodes, not the storage volume or output.
These encrypt the training volume and the model artifacts with the customer managed key.
takeaway: Job security settings: KMS keys for volume/output, VPC config, network isolation.

question: A model deployment pipeline deploys to a staging endpoint first. Which TWO automated checks should run before the production stage? (Select TWO.)
options: A manual approval that a team lead gives after reading the training job’s logs
A load test that confirms latency and error rates meet targets
Skipping tests when the model accuracy improved
Increasing the production instance count to the maximum
Integration tests that call the staging endpoint with known inputs
explanations: A manual review isn’t an automated check, and training logs don’t test the deployed endpoint.
Load tests catch capacity and performance problems before users do.
Accuracy doesn’t prove the endpoint works.
Over-provisioning isn’t a test.
Integration tests catch serialization and contract errors.
takeaway: Before prod: integration tests + load/latency tests on staging.

question: New labeled data arrives in an S3 prefix at unpredictable times, and the team wants the retraining pipeline to start automatically each time a new file lands. Which solution requires the LEAST custom code?
options: A CloudTrail Lake query that runs every hour
An EventBridge rule on S3 Object Created events
A cron job on an EC2 instance that lists the prefix every minute
A manual run in Studio when someone notices new files
explanations: Hourly queries add delay and complexity.
S3 events delivered to EventBridge can start a SageMaker pipeline directly.
Polling needs a server and custom code.
Manual runs aren’t automated.
takeaway: New data in S3 → EventBridge (Object Created) → start pipeline.

question: A team tracks models in MLflow on SageMaker AI and wants deployment code to always fetch “the current production model” without hard-coding version numbers. What should it use?
options: The newest version number, whichever it is
The run ID of the first experiment
A spreadsheet that lists the production version
A model alias, such as champion
explanations: The newest version may not be approved for production.
The first run is rarely the production model.
Manual lists drift from reality.
Aliases let code reference a role (champion) while the version behind it changes.
takeaway: Stable references to changing versions → model aliases (MLflow) or approval status (Model Registry).

question: A team uses Bedrock Flows with Prompt Management. It wants the production app to switch to a new flow version only after testing, and to roll back instantly if needed. How should the app reference the flow?
options: By an alias that points to a tested flow version
By the working draft of the flow
By rebuilding the flow from scratch for each release
By copying the flow’s prompts into the application code
explanations: Aliases can be moved to a new version or back to an old one without app changes.
Drafts change as developers edit them.
Rebuilding loses version history.
Copies drift and need code deployments to change.
takeaway: Flows and prompts: immutable versions + aliases for promotion and rollback.

question: A team wants every merge to its agent repository to deploy the agent to a staging AgentCore Runtime endpoint, run a scripted set of test conversations, and only then update the production endpoint. Which design fits?
options: Developers deploy from their laptops after merging
CodePipeline: deploy, test invocations, then promote the endpoint
Point production at DEFAULT so it gets each latest version
A nightly Lambda function that redeploys the agent from the main branch
explanations: Manual deploys aren’t repeatable or gated.
Automating deploy, test, and promotion gates every change.
DEFAULT changes on every update, skipping the test gate.
Nightly redeploys don’t test each change.
takeaway: Agent CI/CD: deploy → test invocations → promote the named production endpoint.

question: Before each release, a team wants to check automatically that its assistant still resists jailbreak attempts and doesn’t leak PII. Which approach fits a CI pipeline?
options: Run stored adversarial prompts and fail on any that get through
Check that the prompt file has no spelling errors
Measure average latency under load
Ask one tester to try a few jailbreaks by hand each quarter before release
explanations: Automated adversarial tests catch safety regressions before release.
Spelling doesn’t measure safety.
Latency doesn’t test safety.
Manual, infrequent testing misses regressions.
takeaway: Safety regression tests: adversarial prompt suites in CI with pass/fail checks.

question: A team fine-tunes a Bedrock model monthly. Each job creates a new custom model. The team wants the application to move to the new model only after it beats the current one on an evaluation set. Which TWO steps should the release pipeline include? (Select TWO.)
options: Compare the training loss of the new job with the previous job and promote the lower one
Run the same evaluation job on the new and current custom models and compare scores
Switch the app’s model ID only when the new model wins
Delete the current custom model before evaluating the new one
Overwrite the base model with the fine-tuned weights
explanations: Training loss doesn’t show quality on held-out data; compare evaluation scores.
